articles.title: Logos Dev Update: October 2026
articles.subtitle: Your monthly update on the development of the Logos technology stack.
articles.summary: October was a month of hardening and measurement following the Testnet v0.3 release, strengthening decentralised sequencing and publishing benchmarks for service discovery and the Logos Oracle Network.
articles.summaryHtml: October was a month of hardening and measurement following the Testnet v0.3 release, strengthening decentralised sequencing and publishing benchmarks for service discovery and the Logos Oracle Network.
articles.bodyHtml:
Logos provides monthly updates on the state of the technology stack and the development of its various modules, giving developers a clear snapshot of what has been built over the past month.

October was a month of hardening and measurement following the Testnet v0.3 release, with decentralised sequencing strengthened after a testnet incident and benchmark results published for both service discovery and the Logos Oracle Network.

The updates listed here are some of the most important highlights from the past month. Work progresses on many facets of the stack simultaneously, and a more complete, technical breakdown is available at roadmap.logos.co.

For developer-focused highlights on X, please follow Logos Tech. For broader updates on the Logos movement as a whole, stay tuned to the main Logos account.

The Logos Execution Zone

Decentralised sequencing, which arrived with Testnet v0.3, was hardened over the month following a testnet incident. Sequencer restarts no longer trigger incorrect slashing, and chain consistency was improved alongside it.

Transactional actors also merged, bringing atomic composition and asynchronous messaging across both public and private execution. Wallet storage is now encrypted with the wallet password, and the first stage of incremental state updates landed as part of the v0.3 release, introducing a restricted program surface that lays the groundwork for programs producing incremental updates. That last change is a breaking one for both the execution environment and the zone The second and final stage of rolling out the new programming model will be completed with testnet v0.4, after when the LEZ programming model is planned to be stable going forwards.

Zone SDK

The Zone SDK now runs over Logos Protocol. A new backend in the Logos Blockchain Module communicates with Bedrock through the blockchain module, giving the Logos Execution Zone an end-to-end path over the protocol.

Two additions extend what zones can offer their users. Transactions are now automatically refunded on timeout, and withdrawals and transfers support m-of-n signatures.

Logos Blockchain

The mempool now implements the Mempool LIP, with the supporting work merged across the node. λSQL writes are batched into shared inscriptions, raising write throughput, and Blend's connection monitoring was rebuilt around a new layer that applies connection-level rate limiting with observation windows persisting across reconnects.

Nimbos, the Nim client for the Logos Blockchain, now broadcasts blocks and transactions over GossipSub. Validation and relay were added for Cryptarchia block proposals and Mantle transactions, migration to the unified nim-bincode codec is complete, and both P2P and AutoNAT were tested.

Service discovery

Benchmark results confirm that a rare service, offered by only one node in two hundred, is consistently discovered in under 1.5 seconds.

The module was also validated end to end as a Logos Delivery plugin, running on the test fleet with deployed module artefacts.

RLN membership and Poseidon2

A first draft of the RLN Membership Zone RFC, together with an example implementation, is now available in the new logos-rln-membership-zone repository.

Static analysis of the new Poseidon2 circuits has been merged into Zerokit and circom-rln. Poseidon2 is the hash behind RLN's zero-knowledge proofs, and static analysis catches circuit-level correctness issues before they ship.

Logos Oracle Network performance

A performance analysis of the Logos Oracle Network found that a two-minute push cadence keeps the published BTCUSDT price within 0.5 per cent of market in 99.75 per cent of windows, measured across twenty days of Binance data.

The exceptions, roughly one window in four hundred, cluster in short bursts around US macro-release hours.

Logos' readiness for security threats

A new discussion has opened on the research forum examining Logos' readiness for security threats. It responds to Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake, who has called on the industry to prepare for the possibility that a cryptography-breaking discovery arrives sooner than expected, and that it may never be announced at all.

The post is the first of two, with a second covering the Logos Blockchain to follow.

Logos Broadcast Network and Circles

Throughout October, Logos contributors continued to host online and IRL Circles around the world, creating digital and physical space to solve real-world problems with privacy-preserving technology.

The Logos Broadcast Network continued to deliver regular programming, from Dev Club sessions and weekly technical updates to office hours every Friday at 14:00 UTC. Join these office hours to learn more about building on the Logos stack or to get help with specific issues.

Full schedules and participation details are available at press.logos.co/calendar and logos.co/circles. For a full list of upcoming Logos events, check out the event page on Luma.

To get the latest developer updates from the Logos stack, follow Logos Tech on X. Stay tuned to the main Logos account for news on the wider global movement.

articlesFromSameAuthors.title: PriFi: Security and Privacy Against Transactional Hazards
articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Exploring two complementary protections against opportunism inside transactions and predation from outside them
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: Transactions face two distinct classes of hazards: opportunism from participants in the exchange and predation from those outside it. Protecting against each requires a different approach. Security constrains or deters actors positioned to exploit the transaction, while privacy denies outside observers the information needed to target it. PriFi combines both protections across the entire transaction lifecycle.

articlesFromSameAuthors.title: From Motivational to Imperative: Strengthening Commitments with PriFi
articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Making commitments credible through structural design choices
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: Institutions have spent centuries developing ways to inspire faith in the promises they make about future conduct. Typically, these have involved incentives. However, cryptonetworks demonstrated an alternative: strengthening commitments by incorporating them into a system’s architecture.

articlesFromSameAuthors.title: PriFi and the Incomplete Institution: Securing the Transaction Supply Chain
articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Extending imperative credibility beyond transaction settlement to reduce risks and costs
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: Blockchains solved one of the oldest economic problems: how to make a promise hold even when the party making it would prefer otherwise. But transactions do not begin or end at settlement. If security is concentrated at the moment value moves, while information and discretion remain exposed everywhere around it, the transaction remains vulnerable. PriFi aims to secure the entire transaction supply chain.

articles.bodyHtml:
Field Station / Rajasthan: A living experiment in parallel society building

In October, Logos and Zu-Grama brought 30 builders, researchers, activists, and community organisers together for Field Station / Rajasthan, an eight-day experiment in parallel organising at Dhun, a regenerative farm in Jaipur district. Through living, working, and building together, residents explored what a parallel society could look like in practice: communities with the tools and shared responsibility to organise, cooperate, and solve problems for themselves.

The residency connected that mission to local challenges, producing 15 projects, using Logos Basecamp, four winning prototypes and eight submissions for the Zu-Grama d/acc track. From the winners, Offline Zcash explores private payments without an internet connection; Bosphorus enables private lending inside Logos Basecamp; Pukaar lets residents report issues and verify completed repairs; and Dhun Commons provides a shared treasury and coordination tool for farmers and land stewards.

Each winning team will receive milestone-based grant funding and mentoring from Logos and Zu-Grama to further develop its prototype. Connecting the projects with Logos Circles will give local communities opportunities to help shape and use the tools, extending the experiment beyond the residency. The wider cohort will continue working together through reviews, monthly meet-ups, and shared follow-up builds.

You can learn more about Field Station / Rajasthan and the projects that emerged from it in upcoming articles and case studies on Logos Blog.

Nick Merrill: From Fighting Surveillance to Building Alternatives

Last month, we spoke with Nick Merrill, the internet service provider who challenged an FBI demand for customer records, resulting in a gag order that prevented him from discussing it. In the interview, Nick recounts his decade-long legal battle and how it shaped his work building tools to protect people’s privacy.

Surveillance agencies will keep seeking access to our data. Nick’s experience shows why privacy must be built into the infrastructure we use, limiting what can be collected, exposed, or handed over in the first place.

Read more about Nick’s story.

Experience corruption through Nedu’s choices  

“Life’s Choices” continues with Nedu, a young non-profit worker determined to improve his community in Lagos, Nigeria. You make his major decisions as a local clean up grows into an ambition to make changes at the national level, navigating demands for bribes, funding with strings attached, and pressure to stay quiet when money goes missing. His story explores how corruption constrains even our best intentions, and why we need systems that make abuse harder to conceal.

Nedu completes the Present chapter of the “Past. Present. Future.” initiative. Next, we look ahead to the Future, exploring the value of our money in the years to come. Look out for more information. 

For now, play Nedu’s story and see where your decisions take him.

Help curate the Museum of Civil Liberties

In September, we launched the Museum of Civil Liberties, an online archive of major events that shaped history and resulted in the stripping of our personal freedoms. We’re now asking visitors to contribute new exhibits to the museum to bring light to more memories that are too important to be forgotten.  

If you have a historical event to contribute, head to the museum website and fill in the submission form.

Tech highlights

In October, the technical teams focused on strengthening and measuring what shipped with Testnet v0.3. After brief disruption to the testnet, decentralised sequencing was hardened to function better under restarts.

Benchmarks confirmed service discovery reliability, with services offered by only one node in 200 consistently discovered in under a second and a half. Separately, the price feed stayed within 0.5% of the market in 99.75% of cases across 20 days of data.

The Nimbos client also began sharing blocks and transactions across the network, a step towards having more than one independent implementation of the software running.

Contributors opened a discussion on how prepared Logos would be in the event that today’s cryptography is broken by quantum computing sooner than expected, responding to a call from the wider industry to take the risk seriously.

Stay tuned for the October Logos developer update, which will go into more detail and be live very soon.

IRL / Upcoming

Freequencies gears up for round two

The next edition of Freequencies will take place at Damas in Lisbon on 25 November to advance the sovereign coordination tool being built.

Expect a round-table discussion on parallel organising within the local scene, with input from the participating collectives, promoters, and event organisers building for the underground the initiative supports. 

There will be live performances by Perolidade and Oseias. Also, Collective Unconscious and Postcarbon will present Radio-Stesia, a new audiovisual installation centred around biology, technology, coding, and absurdism.

We’ll be sharing more details ahead of the event, so stay tuned.

Logos Circles

October highlights

Logos Circles are open, community-driven spaces where people come together to address challenges in their local communities. Through grassroots collaboration, they create practical solutions, build connections with the broader movement, and use Logos technologies wherever they can strengthen and support their efforts.

More about Circles / Find a Circle near you / Propose a new Circle

In October, Circles formed in:

/ Delhi / Wukari / Portharcourt / Awka / Lagos / Zaria / Yola / Kano / Ruse / Zanzibar / Ede / Abuja / Maiduguri / Kampala / Khartoum / Gombe / Jos / Benin City / Calabar / Katsina / Monrovia / Kaduna / Sokoto / Zaria / Warri / Minna / Aba / Lokoja / Lagos / Zanzibar / Enugu / Damaturu / Bauchi / Algiers / Maraba / Keffi

Check the Logos Forum for individual progress updates on each Circle’s winnable issues.

Logos Circle / Kaduna welcomes students back to school

In October, Logos Circle / Kaduna completed its monthly winnable issue with a back-to-school outreach at Gadol-Chen Academy Nursery and Secondary Education. The Circle engaged more than 200 students and distributed over 200 exercise books, 50 maths sets, over 80 pairs of socks, 400 pens, and four whiteboards to support learning.

Alongside the materials, the Circle introduced students to Logos and discussed education, teamwork, and how people can work together to address community challenges. Coordinated and supported by DJFL Foundation, with additional writing materials from Pristine High School, the outreach brought together local partners to meet practical school needs and encourage students to take an active role in their communities.

More information.

Logos Circle / City Keffi expands access to menstrual health education

On 31 October, Logos Circle / Keffi held its Period with Dignity initiative in the Highcourt community in Keffi, Nasarawa State. Three Circle volunteers delivered sessions in English and Hausa for 35 teenage girls, covering menstrual health, hygiene, and common misconceptions. The outreach also included practical demonstrations of sanitary pad use and provided menstrual hygiene kits to every participant.

Open discussions gave participants space to raise personal concerns and ask things they had previously felt unable to discuss. Questions about affordable alternatives to disposable pads highlighted the financial barriers some girls face, reinforcing the need to combine education with practical support. In response to participants’ requests, the Circle plans to organise a follow-up session and seek partnerships with schools and healthcare professionals to sustain the initiative.

More information.

Several Logos Circles are still finalising their November meetups. For the latest updates, check the Logos events calendar or the Circles discussion channel later in the month.

No Circle in your area yet? Start one.

Logos Media

Blog

The Logos Blog shares technical updates, movement news, and longer-form perspectives on parallel organising and the ideas that shape it. If you have a topic or point of view you’d like to contribute, send us a proposal.

In October, we published: 

  • Mitigating Hazards from Inside and Outside Transactions with PriFi
  • Setting the Collective Action Snowball in Motion: A Journey in Liberland
  • EmPoWering: Joining Logos Blockchain Without an Intermediary
  • PriFi: Security and Privacy Against Transactional Hazards
  • Nick Merrill: The FBI Letter He Couldn’t Tell Anyone About

Local Area Network

The October edition of Local Area Network, the Logos zine, is out now. Inside: stories about Logos Circle / Benin Circle paying medical bills so two families could get discharged from hospital, Logos Circle / Idaban cleaning up its community environment without waiting for permission, Logos Circle / Kampala moving books onto Logos Blockchain, and information about mining Logos Testnet tokens via EmPoWering.

Local Area Network publishes every month and documents the movement. It brings together stories from Logos Circles, practical uses of Logos technology, and arguments about the systems we’re building and those we’re leaving behind. It’s a look at how people are putting these ideas into practice and what they’re learning along the way. 

Read Local Area Network 02, print it, and pass it on.

Logos Broadcast Network

Every month, the Logos Broadcast Network connects voices from throughout the movement, creating space to share knowledge, ideas, and diverse perspectives. Its programming spans community discussions, developer-focused livestreams, explorations of new approaches to coordination, and in-depth conversations about the Logos stack and the technologies shaping its development.

Check the Logos Broadcast Network calendar to see upcoming streams.

Ideas

Each Thursday, the Logos Broadcast Network brings together voices from across the movement and allied organisations to exchange ideas and perspectives. These discussions explore the principles behind parallel societies, reclaiming agency, and protecting freedoms through decentralised, local-first technologies.

On the last Thursday of each month, the Sovereignty Superspace welcomes Parallel Society coalition partners and leading voices in tech and activism to explore strategies for parallel organising.

October streams included: 

  • Agorism & the Crypto-Anarchist Toolkit (with Sal the Agorist)
  • Debasement and Decline: Rome, the Dollar, and the Parallel Society (with Metellus Pius)
  • Sovereignty Superspace (with Jarrad Hope, Amir Taaki, Harry Halpin, and Sal the Agorist)

Follow Logos on X or YouTube to join these discussions every Thursday.

Technical

The Logos Broadcast Network also bridges the gap between developers and the broader community through regular technical livestreams. 

October’s sessions included:

  • Tech Update (proof-of-work onboarding, RLN, decentralised sequencing)
  • Dev Club (proof-of-work onboarding, RLN by default, private multisig)
  • Tech Update (Testnet v0.3 restart)
  • Dev Club (sandboxed AI agents)
  • Dev Club (decentralised 3D printing)
  • Dev Club (private group coordination in Logos Basecamp)

Follow Logos Tech on X and subscribe to the Logos YouTube channel to take part in all the technical streams.

Builder Meetup

Logos Builder Meetups are bi-weekly sessions to help the community better understand, use, and build with the Logos stack. Speak directly with Logos engineers, ask questions, and develop a deeper understanding of the technology stack.

Join every other Friday at 12:00 UTC. The next is 6 November.

Circles

Logos Circle / Online brings together people working to address challenges in their communities each week. Sessions offer practical advice on launching a Logos Circle, alongside firsthand experiences from organisers already turning ideas into action.

Logos Circle / Online is on Tuesdays; join us via the Logos X account or Logos YouTube channel.

Community champions

Logos thrives through the people who build, research, organise, and contribute. Every effort, from technical development to community action, strengthens the network and turns shared ideas into real-world impact.

These are October’s community champions:

  • Punit Pal for writing a Logos node-running guide.
  • Nitish for building an AI agent simulation of Field Station / Rajasthan.
  • Disha for her work on detecting an AI safety failure before it becomes visible.
  • Tuhin for winning the Zu-Grama Field Station track with SignConnect, an AI-powered Indian sign language tool.
  • Nenad for their article on the Liberland clean up.
  • Terricola for their work on Logos Observer.
  • Bristin for their work on the private, serverless forum Forumer.
  • Syafiq for building the LEZ wallet SDK.
  • Uchenna for promoting Logos Circle / Ibadan’s work on the Technies Node blog.
  • Everyone co-living and building at Field Station / Rajasthan.
  • Anyone already running Testnet v0.3 or building on Logos tech.
  • All the stewards hosting Logos Circles in June, and everyone who attended.
  • Anyone else building on Logos tech.
  • Everyone who joined a Logos Broadcast Network stream or read a Logos Blog article.

Your efforts could be featured in an upcoming community spotlight. Technical and non-technical contributions are equally welcome, so share what you’re building, researching, organising, or improving on the forum or Discord. 

Find a way to contribute, create something useful, and help move Logos forward. Build the parallel.

 

Logos builds technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Build the parallel with us.

  • Build on Logos. 
  • Write for Logos Blog.
  • Join a Logos Circle.

articles.title: Building Infrastructure to Privately Create and Sign Transactions
articles.subtitle: A contract is only as secure as the interface within which it is presented.
articles.summary: Logos modules and a local-first interface ensure minimal exposure when creating and signing transactions.
articles.summaryHtml: Logos modules and a local-first interface ensure minimal exposure when creating and signing transactions.

toc.title: How content addressing changes what an interface is
Retrieving an interface is a signal too
The place to build for PriFi

articles.bodyHtml:
A smart contract may be transparent when executing blockchain transactions, but it tells you nothing about the interface through which you draft and sign that transaction - and that interface is where some of the largest losses in this industry have started.

Contracting is the moment an agreement becomes binding. It is also the moment a user hands over authority, almost always by approving something a screen has described to them.

An enormous amount of effort goes into making the contract itself trustworthy. Audits, formal verification and bug bounties are all aimed at the code that executes, which is understandable enough, since that code is permanent, public and expensive to get wrong.

However, almost none of that effort reaches the interface through which the contract is invoked. That interface is fetched from a server, assembled from third-party dependencies, resolved through a domain name and delivered over a connection secured by a certificate authority. Each of those is a party you are trusting, and none of them is visible at the point where you sign.

PriFi is an approach to taking privacy and security across the whole lifecycle of a transaction seriously, reducing exposure every step of the way.

In this article, we will recap the concept of PriFi briefly before looking at the contracting stage of a transaction's lifecycle, and at how Logos Storage and Basecamp point towards a way of delivering interfaces that users control themselves.

What is PriFi?

PriFi (private finance) is an infrastructure design philosophy that aims to make every step of the transaction supply chain private, secure, and immune to leakage. It allows people and institutions to choose to safeguard their identities and information when coordinating, settling, and enforcing transactions.

It is not a single solution and is best understood as an ongoing principle of development for sovereign and privacy-preserving infrastructure, a north star guiding the course for building parallel systems that hand true control to their users.

The lifecycle of a transaction can be seen as seven distinct stages:

In a previous article we covered the first three stages, where two parties find each other, coordinate, and agree what they are going to do. This one looks at the fourth stage - contracting.

Contracting sits between coordination and settlement, and it inherits problems from both. The terms were agreed somewhere, the transaction will be broadcast somewhere, and the interface is what joins those two moments together.

Read our article on private and local-first coordination for more on the first three stages.

Where contracting is exposed

The interface you use to build a transaction is not a fixed object. It is reassembled every time you load it, and it can be different tomorrow, or different for you specifically.

Research into the integrity of modern JavaScript has found that scripts on a significant share of websites change content every single day, and that a client has no reliable way to tell a routine update from a hostile one without information it does not have.

It has already happened at scale. In the Bybit compromise of February 2025, the interface used by the signers was served from cloud storage, its JavaScript was modified, and the injected code was written to activate only when the transaction came from particular contract addresses.

Everyone else saw a perfectly normal application, and the malicious code was removed afterwards.

Roughly $1.5 billion was taken, and the smart contracts were never touched.

Domain names are a second weak point, because they do not really belong to the projects that use them. Curve Finance and Convex Finance have both lost their frontends to DNS compromise while their contracts continued to run exactly as written. In the case of Convex, the change was made by a support agent at the domain registrar, on an account that had two-factor authentication enabled.

The third weak point is the dependency chain. A single compromised package account can inject code into the signing surface of every application that depends on it, none of which has been breached itself, and all of which will serve the result to their users without knowing.

All of this converts into losses at the point of signature. When a wallet cannot decode what it has been handed, the user is asked to approve a screen of unreadable data, and a signature over structured data can hand away spending authority while looking like a harmless message.

In each of these cases, the code that executed was correct, public, and auditable. However, it was not the code that the user expected, as they were trusting a compromised third party.

How content addressing changes what an interface is

Logos Storage is content-addressed file sharing and retrieval. You provide a file to the network and get back a content identifier, and anyone who has that identifier can retrieve the file.

The property that matters for contracting is written into the requirements for the module. Files should be addressable by a content identifier such that users are sure that the content they download is the content they expect.

Applied to a frontend, that can change what an interface for a blockchain transaction is. A content identifier is derived from the bytes it names, so the same identifier resolves to the same interface for everyone who asks for it. Serving one visitor a quietly different page from another is made far more difficult, because a different page generates a different identifier.

Content addressing also changes who can serve an interface. Anyone who has downloaded a file can provide it to others, so an application does not depend on its publisher remaining willing, able, or uncompromised in order to stay reachable.

In future versions of the network, Logos plans to deliver authenticated source and build claims through a package-provenance profile, helping users to verify the packages they import.

Content addressing helps ensure that the bytes match the name you asked for, but does not tell you that the name is the right one – that still needs to be accounted for out-of-band.

As long as you are sure of the CID, you can verify it. Instead of trusting a server, a registrar, a certificate authority and a dependency tree on every single page load, you are trusting the source of the identifier and how it reached you.

The remainder of the interface exposure problem is addressed elsewhere in the stack. The Logos Core package manager specifies cryptographic hashes for packages, verification of file integrity during and after download, and delegatable signing chains for decentralised publisher and authorship integrity.

Retrieving an interface is a signal too

Which interface you fetch is information in its own right. A request for the identifier of a particular exchange's frontend announces what you are about to do before you do it, and content addressing alone does nothing to hide that.

This is where Logos Storage meets the work we covered in our previous article on coordination. Testnet v0.3 introduces downloads over Mix, using a transport layer for relatively larger messages, and running over Logos Mix with RLN.

The goal at this stage of the Logos Testnet is that a node downloading a file should not be linkable to the content it downloads.

The node providing the file is not anonymised yet. Publisher anonymity has been specified but not implemented, and full unlinkability on both sides, with cache nodes able to plausibly deny knowledge of what they hold, is a requirement for mainnet rather than for this testnet.

Read the full specification for more information about Mix.

Basecamp and local-first contracting

Content addressing is only as useful as the client that checks it, and a browser is not that client. A browser is built to fetch and execute whatever the server at the other end of a domain name decides to send.

Basecamp is an interface that runs the Logos stack on your own machine. It loads module interfaces as plugins from the modules you have installed, rather than fetching a page from a server each time you want to use one.

There is no domain to hijack, no certificate authority to mis-issue and no hosting provider in the path between you and the application you are signing with.

In Testnet v0.3, the package manager can source module contents through Logos Storage, so what Basecamp loads arrives over the content-addressed network. At this stage of development, indexing and metadata remain on GitHub, and fully decentralised distribution is a later milestone.

Basecamp also loads module interfaces in separate processes, so an application that crashes, or misbehaves deliberately, cannot take the rest of the stack down with it. That is containment rather than verification, and the two are worth keeping distinct.

Download and install Basecamp at logos.co/basecamp.

What is still being built

Much of what is described above is foundational infrastructure rather than a finished product, and the distinction matters.

Logos Storage today is content-addressed file sharing and retrieval. Privacy-preserving filesharing, where neither publisher nor downloader can be identified, is a separate feature still in progress.

Downloads over Mix in Testnet v0.3 will protect the node doing the downloading, although it is important to note that content providers will remain exposed until later work lands.

The storage backend for the package manager is now available and will be steadily improved in future testnets, meaning that users can download packages without relying primarily on GitHub, while fully decentralised distribution and the signing chains that establish publisher integrity are goals for later releases.

These are the primitives that a verifiable contracting flow gets built from. PriFi is a principle of development rather than a product, and Logos infrastructure is being built out with this principle first in mind.

Read more about the architecture of the Logos stack at docs.logos.co.

The place to build for PriFi

An interface you can check for yourself is not a feature that can be added to a hosted application later. It follows from how the application reaches you, which means it has to be designed from the bottom of the stack upwards.

Testnet v0.3 is running now. If you would like to get involved, download Basecamp and run a node on your machine.

If you want to contribute capacity and play a role in the network, check out the node operator guide.

Building infrastructure for everyone is an open, collaborative effort. If you have ideas, objections, or want to understand more about what Logos is building at the edge of PriFi, join the conversation on the Logos forum.

articles.title: Nick Merrill: The FBI Letter He Couldn’t Tell Anyone About
articles.subtitle: In 2004, an FBI agent handed Nick Merrill a letter he wasn't allowed to tell anyone about. Twenty-five years after the PATRIOT Act became law, he tells the whole story.
articles.summary: Three years after 9/11 and the US government's enacted surveillance act (The PATRIOT Act), Nick Merrill - an ISP provider serving customers since the 90's, received a letter from the FBI accompanied by a gag order. He spent years challenging in court. Twenty-five years later, he tells the whole story.
articles.summaryHtml: Three years after 9/11 and the US government's enacted surveillance act (The PATRIOT Act), Nick Merrill - an ISP provider serving customers since the 90's, received a letter from the FBI accompanied by a gag order. He spent years challenging in court. Twenty-five years later, he tells the whole story.

toc.title: Whoever holds the records is exposed

articles.bodyHtml:
25 years ago today, the USA PATRIOT Act was signed into law. The final bill was introduced in the House on 23 October 2001 and passed there 357 to 66 the next day. The Senate passed it 98 to 1 a day later. Among much else, it widened the FBI's power to demand records with a national security letter.

A national security letter is a type of administrative subpoena that requires no warrant and is designed to help law enforcement or intelligence agencies gather information for national security or terrorism investigations.

In 2004, Nick Merrill received one of those letters. Nick ran Calyx Internet Access, an ISP he had started in New York in the mid-1990s, from an office about ten blocks north of the World Trade Centre site.

First came a phone call. As Nick recalls it, the caller said, "I'm calling from the FBI and I have a letter for you". Less than an hour later, an agent was knocking on his office door. The letter, which ran about three pages, asked for records on one of his clients and listed the types of data the FBI wanted. It also included a gag order.

"It said that I could tell no person that they had asked me for this info. And I stopped there," Nick says. "I looked up at the FBI agent and I said, but what about my lawyer?" The agent told him he was only there to deliver the letter and couldn't answer his questions.

Challenging the national security letter

A national security letter doesn’t require any warrant. As Nick says, “the standard for a national security letter is relevance... It's their unilateral declaration of relevance". This was standard practice from government agencies. The Patriot Act's core mechanisms allowed the government to search first and, if challenged at all, forced the target or recipient to prove the search unjustified, in secret, against a "relevance" standard the FBI set for itself.

The gag order had an immediate impact on his personal life. "My parents were both living at that time. I had a girlfriend I'd been with for years. I couldn't tell any of them that any of this stuff was going on. So if I had just disappeared they would have no idea why."

He called a lawyer anyway. "I knew that I could always talk to a lawyer. That's just unquestionable. That is a basic right". 

His business lawyer pointed out that the New York Civil Liberties Union, the New York branch of the ACLU, was one of the ISP's pro bono clients. Nick had hosted its website for free for years. The ACLU and the NYCLU took the case.

What followed was ten years of litigation: about seven years with the ACLU, then three with a law clinic at Yale Law School. The case began in 2004 under a pseudonym as Doe v. Ashcroft. In August 2010, Nick was allowed to say who he was. In September 2015, a federal judge finally lifted the gag order in full.

In his telling, the government lost, appealed, and lost again. "And then what they decided to do was change the law". As Nick describes it, the amended rules let recipients consult a lawyer and gave them a way to challenge a letter in court. 

He doesn't think that fixed the core problem, though: "So all of a sudden now the burden is on the recipient rather than on the government".

He doesn't paint the agencies as villains. 

"I do believe that at least on some level the people in the counterintelligence and anti-terrorism parts of the government really did want to protect the country from threats that were on some level real."

However, he feels strongly that the foundational, bedrock principles enshrined in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights should be protected.

Whoever holds the records is exposed

The FBI reached Nick's customers through Nick because his ISP held their records, and logging their data was the default configuration of his system. 

"The default way that Unix works is it keeps logs of everything that happens," he says. "This is just how things come out of the box. All the systems keep records of everything."

Anyone who relies on a service that keeps records about them carries the same exposure, and so does whoever runs it. 

Logos builds infrastructure that aims to mitigate this risk, by ensuring data and the transport it moves over are private and decentralised.

Nick went on to found the Calyx Institute, a nonprofit named after the ISP, and spent 15 years there building privacy tools such as Tor exit nodes, encrypted chat over Tor, and a version of Android with Tor built in. 

Those years left him with three priorities: to encrypt communications, counter metadata analysis, and counter location tracking.

"At first it seemed like the most important thing is to encrypt the contents of people's communications. But then it became evident that metadata was maybe even more dangerous.”

Metadata privacy has also been an area of interest for Logos, the technology stack and movement for a private and decentralised internet. Logos aims to degrade the ability of observers to reconstruct who talks to whom, when, and how often, even against a sophisticated adversary watching the network.

Logos Chat encrypts conversations end to end, Delivery transports those messages over a peer-to-peer network through a mixnet, and spam resistance is enabled by rate limiting through RLN.

Logos Testnet v0.3 has been live since 30 September and is open for anyone to build and experiment on. In this early stage of deployment, Chat accounts don't yet persist across sessions, and Storage downloads over Mix protect the downloader but not yet the provider.

The interview also touched on the same problem in money, with Corey noting that blockchain settlement is tamper resistant but very transparent. 

On Logos Blockchain, Cryptarchia keeps validator identities and stake hidden, and the Logos Execution Zone (LEZ) supports private accounts and shielded transfers. Base-layer notes on Bedrock stay public, and private balances live on the LEZ.

A journey towards privacy

Nick says that people should view privacy not as a binary feature but as an incremental journey towards better protection online.

"One of the problems I see in the privacy space is just total binary thinking," Nick says. 

"If you gain a 30% increase in privacy over what you had before and you didn't have to give up very much to get it, that's a huge win that allows you to then catch your breath, think of what you're going to do next, then take another step that will get you another 15% more privacy."

He points to encryption in transit. "Virtually all web browsing traffic is encrypted in transit now. These are huge wins that came just in the past 10 or 15 years."

Improving privacy can be as simple as just raising the cost of surveillance. "We can make it economically unfeasible to just mass dragnet surveil everyone,” he says.

If you’re interested in building a more private digital world, you can play your part by installing Basecamp, the launcher for private, peer-to-peer apps built on Logos.

In a future session with Nick Merrill, we will look at Bluetooth mesh networks, post-quantum cryptography, and Phreeli. Post your questions to Nick in the forum thread and he’ll answer them.

Watch the full episode on YouTube.

Join the discussion on the Logos Forum.

Build the parallel.

articlesFromSameAuthors.title: PriFi: Security and Privacy Against Transactional Hazards
articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Exploring two complementary protections against opportunism inside transactions and predation from outside them
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: Transactions face two distinct classes of hazards: opportunism from participants in the exchange and predation from those outside it. Protecting against each requires a different approach. Security constrains or deters actors positioned to exploit the transaction, while privacy denies outside observers the information needed to target it. PriFi combines both protections across the entire transaction lifecycle.

toc.title: Security: Constraining opportunism inside the transaction
Privacy: Preventing predation from outside the transaction
Information as an input for predation
When public information becomes the attack surface
Revealing what is necessary without exposing everything else
Protecting the entire transaction supply chain
PriFi as an architecture of security and privacy

articles.bodyHtml:
Blockchains introduced unprecedented settlement guarantees by embedding rules into the infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on intermediaries' promises. However, as explored in previous articles in this series, securing settlement does not necessarily secure the transaction itself.

Drawing on ideas and research compiled by Logos cofounder Jarrad Hope, we can consider a transaction to comprise seven distinct links: discovery, diligence, negotiation, contracting, ordering, settlement, and enforcement. Each involves the exchange of information, the delegation of authority, or reliance on another actor's conduct. Vulnerabilities can emerge at any of these points, even when the final transfer of value is executed precisely as intended by the underlying protocol.

The third article in the PriFi series distinguished between two hazard classes. The first consists of actors inside the transaction, whose legitimate participation gives them access to information or capabilities they can exploit opportunistically. The second consists of outsiders who acquire information about a transaction and use it to identify opportunities for predation. Both threaten the potential gains from exchange, but the mechanisms through which they operate differ. Therefore, the appropriate protections must differ, too.

This article examines the two corresponding protections: security, which binds and deters those positioned to act against the transaction, and privacy, which limits the information available to actors who have no legitimate reason to possess it. It then considers why neither is sufficient on its own, and how combining them can strengthen the commitments underpinning private finance.

Security: Constraining opportunism inside the transaction

Exchange requires participants to place some degree of trust in one another. A lender must assess a borrower's ability to repay, a buyer must establish that a seller can deliver what was promised, and two parties negotiating a trade must disclose enough information to make an agreement even possible. These disclosures are necessary for exchange, but they also introduce exploitable vulnerabilities.

For example, a buyer might receive goods and subsequently refuse payment. A borrower might misrepresent the quality of their collateral. A counterparty entrusted with assets might exercise authority in a way that was never intended by the original agreement. In each case, the hazard emerges because the transaction grants somebody a position from which they can act against another participant.

Simply concealing information cannot eliminate this problem. A lender cannot assess a loan without learning something about the borrower, while a buyer cannot make an informed purchase without knowing something about the goods being offered. Instead, the problem is to make opportunistic behaviour sufficiently difficult, expensive, or unattractive, ensuring the transaction can proceed with reasonable confidence.

Making defection costly

Historically, commercial institutions have developed an extensive range of mechanisms for constraining opportunistic behaviour. Contracts create enforceable obligations, collateral places valuable assets at risk, escrow arrangements limit unilateral control over funds, and reputational consequences discourage misconduct among parties expecting to transact again. These mechanisms work by changing the incentives facing somebody who might otherwise defect.

Consider a landlord requiring a deposit from a tenant. The deposit does not physically prevent damage to the property. Rather, it increases the financial consequences of causing damage or failing to fulfil certain contractual obligations. The tenant retains the capacity to act opportunistically, but the expected cost of doing so rises.

A similar principle applies to commercial performance bonds. A contractor undertaking a substantial project may be required to provide a bond that protects the customer against specified failures to perform. The bond does not guarantee that the contractor will complete the work, but it changes the allocation of financial risk and increases the consequences of underperforming. Such mechanisms create what previous articles in this series have described as motivational credibility. The actor retains the discretion to defect, but has reasons not to exercise it.

Their limitation is that those reasons remain contingent. If the gains from defection become sufficiently large, the probability of punishment sufficiently small, or the actor sufficiently indifferent to future consequences, opportunistic behaviour may still become attractive. Security must, therefore, consider an actor's capacity to defect and the likelihood that they can do so with impunity.

Removing discretion to defect

Cryptonetworks introduced another possibility: instead of making a prohibited action expensive, infrastructure can make particular actions impossible under the system's enforced rules.

Consider a transaction in which two parties wish to exchange different assets. Under a conventional arrangement, one party may have to transfer their asset first and trust the other to complete the exchange. This exposes the first participant to the possibility that their counterparty will receive the asset and refuse to reciprocate. An escrow service can mitigate the problem, but it introduces another actor whose conduct must itself be trusted or constrained.

Atomic swaps illustrate how some of this dependence can instead be addressed through protocol design. Maurice Herlihy's research into atomic cross-chain swaps describes mechanisms through which parties can coordinate exchanges without relying on a single participant's discretionary promise to complete their side of the trade. Using cryptographic conditions and time restrictions, protocols can be designed to structurally protect against specified forms of counterparty defection (Herlihy, 2018). Such architectures ensure that a counterparty cannot simply receive the other party's asset while disregarding the conditions governing the exchange. Rather than relying entirely on reputational or contractual consequences, the system constrains the actions available to participants.

This illustrates imperative credibility: certain commitments are enforced structurally rather than sustained exclusively through incentives. However, imperative credibility does not eliminate every possible hazard. Software defects, compromised signing processes, misleading interfaces, governance decisions, and operational dependencies can still create opportunities for exploitation. The protection applies to the actions actually constrained by the architecture, not to every circumstance surrounding the transaction.

Security should not be understood as a single mechanism applied at settlement. It requires identifying the capabilities each actor possesses throughout the transaction lifecycle, determining which could be abused, and reducing unnecessary discretion wherever possible. The architecture for enhancing security should, therefore, seek to limit the ability to defect, increase the costs of misconduct where discretion remains necessary, and reduce the opportunities to act without accountability.

Privacy: Preventing predation from outside the transaction

The second hazard class presents a different challenge. An external predator has not necessarily entered into an agreement with the participants. They may have accepted no contractual obligations, placed no collateral at risk, and developed no reputational relationship with the people whose transaction they intend to exploit. As a result, the mechanisms available for controlling opportunistic counterparties may be ineffective against them.

A contract cannot meaningfully bind an unknown observer who never agreed to its terms. Nor can a reputation-based mechanism reliably deter an attacker who can act anonymously, disappear afterwards, or operate beyond the reach of the institutions expected to punish them. Security may still limit an outsider's ability to attack, but there is another way to reduce the hazard: prevent them from acquiring the information necessary to identify the opportunity in the first place.

Information as an input for predation

As established in the previous article, an outside actor generally requires some combination of information, capacity, and impunity to exploit a transaction. Information allows the actor to identify a target or opportunity. Capacity determines whether they can act upon it. Impunity affects the expected consequences of doing so. These conditions offer a useful way to understand the economics of predation.

Consider a company preparing to acquire a competitor. If the negotiations remain confidential, outside traders may have no reason to anticipate the acquisition. Once information about the impending deal leaks, however, traders can potentially acquire shares before the announcement moves their price. The ability to trade existed all along, but information becoming available may alert observers to a particular opportunity.

Similar considerations apply in procurement, where revealing bids before an auction closes can allow competitors to respond strategically to information they would otherwise lack. William Vickrey's research into auctions and competitive sealed tenders provides an important foundation for understanding how auction rules shape bidder incentives and the use of information (Vickrey, 1961).

A sealed-bid auction deliberately restricts what participants know about competing offers. The objective is not to eliminate information from the transaction, but to control when and to whom it becomes available. Importantly, a conventional sealed-bid auction may still require trusting the auctioneer to preserve confidentiality. Researchers have consequently explored cryptographic auction designs in which a winning bid can be determined without revealing losing bids to either the auctioneer or other bidders (Peralta, Montenegro, & Lopez, 2013).

This illustrates the relationship between privacy and credible commitments. Concealing information from competitors reduces opportunities for strategic exploitation, while constraining the auctioneer's access to that information reduces dependence on their continued restraint. Both protections contribute to the integrity of the exchange, but they address different positions from which exploitation could occur.

When public information becomes the attack surface

Transparent blockchains make the informational dimension of predation particularly important. Transaction histories, wallet balances, contract interactions, and in many systems, pending transaction intentions can be observed by those with no relationship to the participants involved. This information may be valuable for verification, but it can also significantly reduce the cost of identifying targets.

Address poisoning illustrates the problem. In this attack, an adversary examines a wallet's transaction history and generates a new address that resembles one the wallet has previously interacted with. The attacker then attempts to introduce the deceptive address into the victim's transaction history, hoping that a future payment will be misdirected.

Chainalysis documented a May 2024 case in which approximately $68 million in wrapped BTC was transferred to an attacker-controlled lookalike address. The funds were subsequently returned, but the incident demonstrates how publicly available transaction information can support highly targeted deception (Chainalysis, 2024). The attacker did not need to compromise the blockchain's settlement rules. Instead, they exploited information about previous interactions and the user's reliance on transaction history when preparing a new transfer. This demonstrates an important limitation of privacy as a defence: preventing unnecessary exposure of information can reduce an attacker's ability to select and manipulate a target, but it does not eliminate the need for secure transaction verification.

The same pattern appears in decentralised trading. Philip Daian and others documented how bots exploit observable transactions and compete for favourable execution ordering when interacting with automated market maker decentralised exchanges. Their research demonstrated how transaction visibility and ordering discretion can create opportunities to capture value from other market participants, also known as MEV (Daian et al., 2020).

Consider an investor submitting a large token purchase to the blockchain. If the order is publicly visible before execution, another participant may be able to buy ahead of it, benefit from the resulting price movement, and sell afterwards. The investor's transaction may settle correctly under the protocol's rules, yet still deliver a worse economic outcome because information about the intended trade was known before settlement. 

For such an attack, the adversary need not know the investor's real-world identity. The existence, size, and intended execution of the order may be sufficient. Privacy, therefore, concerns more than concealing personal information. It means limiting the disclosure of any information that gives unrelated actors an exploitable advantage.

Security and privacy: Complementary protections

The two protections target different hazards, but they should not be treated as independent alternatives. Security principally addresses what an actor can do and the consequences of doing it. Privacy principally addresses what an actor can know, and whether that knowledge enables them to identify an opportunity for exploitation.

These mechanisms do not map perfectly onto the two hazard classes. An outsider's ability to act can be constrained by security mechanisms, while privacy can also protect sensitive information from counterparties. Nevertheless, the distinction helps establish where each protection is most economically useful.

A counterparty who must receive information to complete an exchange cannot simply be denied all access. Their behaviour must also be constrained. Conversely, the best defence against an outside observer with no legitimate need to know about the transaction may be to prevent the information from reaching them at all. The difference becomes especially clear when either protection is applied in isolation.

Security without privacy

Imagine an institution holding a substantial quantity of digital assets in a wallet protected by multiple independent signatures. Its authorisation structure may make unilateral theft extremely difficult. No single actor has sufficient authority to move the funds, and the underlying blockchain will reject transfers that do not meet the wallet's execution conditions.

However, if the institution's holdings, transaction patterns, and operational relationships are publicly observable, outside actors may still acquire useful information about where to concentrate their efforts. They might target signatories with phishing attempts, monitor operational patterns, or attempt to compromise systems involved in preparing transactions. The security controls remain valuable, but the information available to attackers can make those controls more expensive to maintain.

Privacy without security

Now consider the reverse. A financial institution moves its transactions into a confidential environment, shielding counterparties, balances, and trading intentions from public observation. However, the service provider maintaining that environment retains unrestricted access to transaction information and possesses the authority to alter, delay, or disclose it. The institution has reduced exposure to unrelated outsiders, but has concentrated privileged information and discretion in a new actor. The security of the transaction depends on that actor continuing to exercise its authority appropriately.

As the second article in this series argued, this remains a motivational commitment. The provider may have strong commercial and legal incentives to behave correctly, but the ability to defect has not necessarily been removed. The result is privacy from the public without equivalent protection against an insider. Neither outcome is sufficient for an infrastructure-design philosophy seeking to minimise both the risk of exploitation and the costs of mitigating that risk.

Revealing what is necessary without exposing everything else

Combining security and privacy creates a new challenge: legitimate transactions require certain information to be disclosed. A lender needs assurance that collateral exists. An exchange needs to establish that assets are available for transfer. A regulator or auditor may need evidence that particular obligations have been satisfied. Absolute privacy would make some of these activities impossible or introduce significant new risks of misrepresentation.

The objective is, therefore, not to conceal everything, but to distinguish the information required to perform or verify a legitimate function from information exposed merely because the underlying infrastructure makes it observable. Modern cryptography offers mechanisms for making this distinction more practical.

Zero-knowledge proofs, for example, allow one party to demonstrate that a particular statement is true without revealing the underlying information used to establish it. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology describes this as a way for a prover to convince a verifier of a statement without disclosing additional information beyond its truth (NIST, n.d.).

Consider a borrower seeking to establish that they satisfy a collateral threshold. In a conventional arrangement, the lender may request detailed records showing the borrower's assets. In a suitably designed cryptographic system, it may instead be possible to prove that specified assets satisfy the required threshold without disclosing every holding or transaction in the borrower's financial history. The lender receives evidence relevant to the agreement, while unrelated information can remain concealed.

This does not eliminate the need to verify that the assets are genuinely controlled by the borrower, correctly valued, and available as collateral. Nor does it remove the possibility of risks beyond the particular statement being proved. However, it demonstrates that verifiability and universal information disclosure need not be the same thing.

Other techniques, including encrypted communications, cryptographic commitments, secure multiparty computation, and selective disclosure, offer different ways to distribute information according to the needs of a transaction. Each addresses a particular problem. Encryption can protect communications from observers without necessarily hiding who is communicating. A commitment can fix a value without immediately revealing it, although the value may subsequently need to be disclosed. Secure multiparty computation can enable participants to evaluate certain functions over private inputs without revealing those inputs to one another. 

The broader design opportunity is to provide the information necessary for an exchange while reducing the additional exposure created by the infrastructure carrying it out. For PriFi, the goal is to make transactions appropriately verifiable without making every commercially sensitive detail available to every observer.

Protecting the entire transaction supply chain

The distinction between security and privacy becomes more useful when applied across the seven links of the transaction lifecycle. During discovery, privacy can prevent a participant's search for counterparties from revealing commercially valuable intentions to unrelated observers. Security, meanwhile, can provide mechanisms for authenticating participants and reducing the likelihood of fraudulent introductions.

During diligence, selective disclosure and cryptographic proofs can limit the information participants must surrender, while verification and enforceable obligations help address misrepresentation.

During negotiation, confidential communications protect bargaining positions from outside exploitation, while agreed procedures and authenticated messages can reduce opportunities for manipulation or disputes over what was communicated. 

During contracting, cryptographic commitments and digital signatures can make agreed-upon terms verifiable, while access controls can reduce the unnecessary disclosure of those terms.

During ordering, concealing pending transaction intentions can reduce opportunities for frontrunning, while mechanisms that constrain the discretion of those responsible for sequencing transactions can address another potential source of exploitation.

At settlement, protocol-enforced validity conditions can prevent unauthorised state transitions, while privacy-preserving transaction designs can reduce unnecessary disclosures concerning balances, counterparties, and asset movements.

Finally, enforcement may require verifiable evidence of agreed obligations and mechanisms for resolving disputes, without necessarily publishing the parties' complete financial relationships.

These examples demonstrate why securing an individual blockchain function is not equivalent to securing the transaction. If discovery exposes an investor's intentions, private settlement may come too late to protect them from strategic responses. If negotiation is confidential, but the application used to prepare a transaction can substitute malicious instructions, privacy will not prevent an unauthorised outcome. If settlement conceals balances but a central infrastructure provider can observe every request, the exposure has merely been relocated.

Protection must instead be evaluated across the entire lifecycle, considering both the actors capable of exploiting a position and the information that makes the position economically valuable.

PriFi as an architecture of security and privacy

PriFi brings these two approaches together by treating transactional protection as an architectural problem rather than something that can be addressed exclusively through individual applications or voluntary institutional promises. The objective is to reduce two related dependencies: reliance on actors choosing not to misuse their capabilities, and reliance on unrelated observers choosing not to exploit information they can access.

The first can be addressed through security mechanisms that constrain authority, distribute permissions, and make misconduct more difficult or costly. The second can be addressed through privacy mechanisms that minimise unnecessary disclosure of information and reduce the number of actors who can observe sensitive activity. This is consistent with the broader objective of Logos, whose architecture combines locally operated applications with privacy-preserving networking, messaging, storage, and blockchain infrastructure.

A locally operated application can reduce reliance on hosted infrastructure that can observe or control interactions. Privacy-preserving communications can limit the information exposed while participants coordinate, while protocol-level rules can constrain the subsequent movement of assets. None of these mechanisms provides complete protection on its own. Their value comes from reducing various vulnerabilities that arise as a transaction moves from coordination to execution.

Muster, the experimental application built with the Logos stack and introduced in previous articles, provides a practical setting for examining these dependencies. Making visible the information disclosed during transactional coordination and the infrastructure involved helps distinguish where confidentiality is preserved, where authority remains concentrated, and where participants still depend on other actors' conduct.

The broader question is whether these dependencies can be progressively reduced through architectural design. Protecting financial transactions requires more than making promises about intermediaries' behaviour. It also requires considering which actors should possess particular information or capabilities in the first place.

PriFi: Securing transactions structurally

The economic importance of security and privacy extends beyond preventing individual attacks. When participants face uncertainty about whether counterparties will honour agreements, they incur costs to manage that uncertainty. They may require collateral, insurance, intermediaries, extensive diligence, or more complex contractual arrangements.

When they face the additional risk that outside actors can observe and exploit their activity, they may incur further costs to conceal their intentions, protect operational information, or avoid exposing valuable positions. Some participants may ultimately decide that the combined risks and mitigation costs outweigh the expected benefits of transacting at all.

Security and privacy can reduce these barriers through different mechanisms. Security strengthens confidence that actors granted access or authority cannot easily abuse their positions. Privacy reduces the number of external actors who can discover and exploit opportunities created by the transaction. Their combined effect is to reduce the expected cost of transactional hazards, potentially enabling exchanges that would otherwise be too risky or expensive to undertake.

Blockchain demonstrated that the rules governing settlement can be enforced without requiring participants to place unrestricted trust in a central operator. PriFi builds on that by asking how similarly credible protections can be extended across the information flows, relationships, and dependencies surrounding settlement.

The objective is not absolute privacy, nor the elimination of every possible risk. It is to ensure that the information and authority required for exchange are distributed only as far as necessary, and constrained wherever possible.

toc.title: No on-ramp needed to start using Logos
Privacy and sovereignty from the start

articles.bodyHtml:
Every blockchain asks something of a newcomer before it lets them take part. Posting a transaction costs a fee, and so does sending a message through a privacy layer, so a participant who arrives with nothing cannot use the network at all.

Most networks solve this with an intermediary. A testnet usually relies on a faucet run by the project, while a live network relies on exchanges and bridges, which is understandable enough, since they are the simplest way to put tokens into someone's hands.

However, every one of those intermediaries decides whether you may take part, and every one of them keeps a record of who you are and when you arrived. On a network designed to protect its participants, that record is created before any protection can set in.

EmPoWering, introduced in Testnet v0.3, is the proof-of-work mechanism that removes the intermediary from Logos Blockchain. It lets anyone obtain testnet tokens from the network, and send messages through the Blend Network, by performing computational work on their own machine.

Not only does this approach enhance privacy for new participants – it also allows applications to remove friction and deliver a better user experience by onboarding users to token-linked apps without requiring them to transfer an initial amount of tokens.

In this article, we will explore how EmPoWering works and what it means for privacy and sovereignty.

Private entry without third parties

Every conventional route into a network requires a transfer that leaves a trace. An exchange typically requires identity checks and records a payment, a bridge links your new address to an existing one on another chain along with its full history, and even a faucet sees your IP address and often asks for an account or a social media handle.

Whichever route you take, your first address on the network is tied to something that identifies you, and everything you do from that address afterwards inherits the link.

EmPoWering solves this by allowing you to enter the network in a privacy preserving manner  by conducting computations on your own hardware instead of relying on a traceable intermediary. 

You receive tokens from the network through this exercise, which can be transacted on the blockchain or used to participate in the Blend Network, which is designed to prevent block proposers from being linked to their stake as part of the network’s Private Proof-of-Stake consensus.

EmPoWering removes the link to a centralised on-ramp or platform that can connect your identifying information to your new address on Logos. Instead, if you wish, you can simply receive enough tokens through proof-of-work to start transacting on the blockchain, without needing to transfer in from another blockchain or via an on-ramp.

No on-ramp needed to start using Logos

As EmPoWering is further integrated into the ecosystem, the mechanism could also allow applications to offer a more intuitive user experience than traditional blockchain-based applications.

For example, when a new user interacts with an application that relies on RLN, they will need a number of tokens to interact with this system. Instead of transferring tokens from another chain or bridge into their wallet to begin, they can start participating directly by relying on EmPoWering to gain those first tokens. 

App developers could build on this mechanism to allow users to use EmPoWering as part of their setup process, removing the friction often associated with blockchain-related applications. Through integrated EmPoWering, users could easily install and start using private and peer-to-peer apps built on Logos without even needing to worry about moving tokens onto the chain.

In this way, Logos uses Proof-of-Work as an entry point for private and accessible participation, while it relies on its novel Private Proof-of-Stake mechanism for secure consensus.

EmPoWering is not designed to outperform Proof-of-Stake for validator incentives – it is built solely for improving private participation; therefore the two mechanisms complement each other and do not compete.

How EmPoWering works

EmPoWering asks a participant to solve a puzzle. Their machine tries value after value until it finds one whose hash falls below a target, which takes time and electricity.

Checking a solution is valid just requires a single hash, so every node can easily verify the work has been completed. Each puzzle is also tied to recent network state, so solutions cannot be prepared in advance or stored up for later.

In the current version of the Logos Testnet, a proof-of-work solution can be used for either Blend access or to gain testnet tokens, and each use has its own threshold.

For access to the Blend Network, the participant searches for a private value that clears the Blend threshold. That value stays secret, and the proof attached to their messages shows only that they are entitled to send them, so a message backed by computational work looks the same as one from a node that helps run the network.

The Blend threshold is set with modest hardware in mind. At the network's reference level of activity, a solution takes under a minute on average using a single core of a Raspberry Pi 5.

For testnet tokens, the participant tries fresh keys until one clears the claim threshold, then submits a claim transaction. Once the claim is accepted, a fixed amount of testnet tokens goes to that key.

The amount is set to cover the fee for the claim and for a first transfer, so someone arriving with an empty wallet can make the claim without already holding testnet tokens to pay for it.

Read more about EmPoWering in the Logos LIPs.

How the thresholds adjust

The claim threshold follows demand for testnet tokens. After every block it adjusts towards around ten accepted claims per block, so when more people are solving puzzles, each claim takes more work while the number of claims stays steady.

The Blend threshold follows activity across the network. Once per epoch it looks at how many transactions blocks have been carrying, tightening when the network is busy and loosening when it is quiet, with each change capped so it cannot swing sharply from one epoch to the next.

When the network is quiet and there is less ordinary traffic for messages to hide among, the lower threshold lets more participants into the Blend Network, and the traffic they add makes every message harder to single out.

Keeping the two thresholds separate means each can be adjusted independently, with demand for testnet tokens determining the cost of a claim and overall network activity setting the cost of Blend access.

Privacy and sovereignty from the start

EmPoWering removes the moment of exposure that usually comes with joining a network. There is no exchange account, no bridge transfer linking a new address to an old one, and no faucet request tied to an IP address. 

A participant's first testnet tokens arrive at a key connected to nothing else. Additionally, they are able to contribute to the Blend Network without a traceable log or identifying approval, instead simply solving a puzzle to begin sending data and cover traffic.

Verification follows the same principle. Every node checks the work independently, so nobody needs the project, a faucet operator, or any other party to vouch for them.

EmPoWering is new to the testnet, and it is subject to continued development. The thresholds and the amount of testnet tokens available per claim are still being refined, and further adjustments are likely as the testnet runs.

EmPoWering addresses the exposure involved in getting started. Protecting transactions once a participant is inside the network depends on other parts of the stack designed along the principles of private finance.

It is important to note that testnet tokens exist for testing the network, and the testnet may be reset as development continues.

Read more about the launch of Testnet v0.3

Get started with Logos

Testnet v0.3 is live now. If you would like to get involved, download Basecamp and run a node on your machine.

If you want to contribute capacity and play a role in the network, check out the node operator guide.

Building infrastructure for everyone is an open, collaborative effort. 

If you have ideas, objections, or want to understand more about what Logos is building, join the conversation on the Logos forum.
