articles.title: Setting the Collective Action Snowball in Motion: A Journey in Liberland
articles.subtitle: Insights from two Logos-driven community river cleanups
articles.summary: Small acts of collective action can spark a snowball effect, inspiring others to take responsibility for their communities and create meaningful change without waiting for permission. Two community cleanups in Liberland show how small victories can inspire others and build momentum from the ground up.
articles.summaryHtml: Small acts of collective action can spark a snowball effect, inspiring others to take responsibility for their communities and create meaningful change without waiting for permission. Two community cleanups in Liberland show how small victories can inspire others and build momentum from the ground up.
articles.bodyHtml:
As we sat in the meeting point we’d set, on the morning of our first Liberland community cleanup back in April this year, I began to doubt the whole thing. Did we invite enough people? Could we have done anything better? Did the community even care about the place they live? Why was nobody showing up?   

It was my first time at Liberland’s Oasis in Arc Village, and I hadn’t been sure what to expect. We had come for the micronation’s 11th-year anniversary celebrations, hoping to inspire attendees to take action to improve their communities without bureaucracy, red tape, or waiting for permission. We’d talked about it a lot online and off: starting with something simple but organic from the community itself. It doesn’t matter if the feedback loop is small to begin with; winning on issues will inspire others, and with more people, we can take on bigger problems.

At least that was the theory we were working with, but the scant turnout had me second-guessing all that.

As the meeting time approached, some volunteers did show up – fewer than hoped for, but at least we now had a team to devise a plan with. Equipped with bags, rubbish pickers, and not-so-protective gloves, we headed down to the banks of the Danube and got to work tackling the waste that had been building up for years. What we lacked in numbers, we made up for in positive energy, filling more than 35 rubbish bags from the area.

Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find a local steward to continue the work after we left. However, a radio station picked up the story, and our post documenting the cleanup received more than 600 likes and 70 comments in a Facebook community group for the area. The President of Liberland even gave us a shoutout. 

We left reassured that we had made an impact, from which maybe future actions could sprout. People did care.

It didn’t matter that they weren’t at the first cleanup. Perhaps they didn’t know how to get involved. Maybe they were waiting for someone else to take the first step. It didn’t really matter. The point was, people reacted. And that showed the problem was real. They appreciated what we were doing. They did care.

So, we decided to return.

A second visit to Liberland

Encouraged by our first expedition’s impact and with plenty of learnings from it, we secured a speaking slot at Liberland’s Floating Man Festival, a seven-day celebration of freedom delivered through music and arts, held in late August. We’d stayed in contact with people from the local community, organised some friends to join us, and wanted to make a very clear statement:

We shouldn’t wait for others to start caring for the places we live.

The second time around, the conditions weren’t exactly on our side. The heat was brutal, and many people from the wider community understandably decided not to join us. Yet, as the meeting spot filled with new and old faces, I felt encouraged. People did care. More people.

We headed down to the banks of the Danube again, our crew having almost doubled in numbers since the first cleanup. The team we’d assembled spanned generations, with the youngest around 14 and the oldest in their mid-60s.

We had music, beers and other refreshments brought along by ourselves and fellow volunteers, and an abundance of positivity. We laughed and conversed as we worked, but mostly focused on the task at hand. The longer we dragged the job out, the longer we’d have to endure the 38-degree August inferno and the longer it’d be before we could reward ourselves with a cold drink under the shade of a tree. By the time I took that first sip, we had gathered more than 50 bags of rubbish from the pathways next to the river.

Radio Danube came to support our efforts again, and I gave my first-ever interview. VidiVamo, a local influencers group that promotes people working to create meaningful change, documented the action, too. These local publicity opportunities are almost as important as the cleanups themselves and should never be passed up. They’re a chance to amplify our work, and discovering that these kinds of initiatives exist is the first step towards people getting involved.

The online responses we received to the second cleanup made things even clearer. Our follow-up post about the collective action received more than 420 likes and 30 comments in the community Facebook group, while another post, “Help Appeal by the Danube”, received more than 150 likes and 20 comments.

It would be easy to look at the bags of rubbish removed and the social metrics and say that the initiative was successful because we made the area cleaner and the posts received engagement. However, the numbers weren’t what stood out to me most; the actual conversations beneath those posts were what really convinced me that we were making a difference and that it was growing.

People started pointing out other problems in the area, other areas overlooked by municipal services. They were starting to think about actions they could take to improve their own community. From the comments, we learned about an informal dumping spot next to a local kindergarten. If rubbish keeps appearing in the same place, you have to ask, “Why?”

Is there infrastructure missing? Are there clear signs discouraging littering? Who is supposed to maintain the area? And, perhaps most importantly, are children growing up learning that caring for the environment is part of caring for each other?

We concluded that something simple, such as installing clear signposts reminding residents and visitors to dispose of their waste responsibly, was an appropriate first response. It’s a basic idea, but sometimes small interventions are exactly where lasting change begins. 

Then came perhaps the most encouraging part of the whole experience – the real proof that what we were doing was having an impact and that impact was snowballing. 

A young couple who had seen our posts documenting the cleanups took it upon themselves to clean up a local creek. They inboxed me to show their efforts, and it was truly inspirational to see our work encouraging others to act.

They didn’t wait for us to organise it. They didn’t wait for someone else to tell them what to do.

They just went and did it, the two of them filling 12 bags of rubbish during an afternoon.

That, to me, is the real point of this kind of action.

A single cleanup isn’t going to solve every environmental problem around the Danube. Fifty bags of rubbish won’t suddenly create a sustainable local ecosystem.

But one word can start a conversation.

A conversation connects people.

And a group of people can take on projects that an individual would struggle to achieve.

And people see others' efforts and want to get involved themselves.

As the snowball gains momentum, it becomes unstoppable.

Decentralised parallel structures aren’t just about creating alternative institutions or talking about sovereignty. They’re also about looking at the place around you and asking: What can I take responsibility for?

True sovereignty begins with shared responsibility for the space we inhabit. That can start with someone seeing something as simple as a normal person picking up a bag of rubbish from a public area and getting inspired to do the same. This is why Logos Circles exist: to provide the infrastructure and networks for grassroots community initiatives, to start taking action without waiting for permission. 

 

Learn more about Logos Circles / Join a Circle near you / Propose a new Circle

articles.title: Mitigating Hazards from Inside and Outside Transactions with PriFi
articles.subtitle: Two hazard classes threaten transactions: those inside the deal and (potentially) everyone else
articles.summary: PriFi , or private finance, is not about absolute secrecy, and it’s not about evading regulations. It’s about user-operated financial infrastructure, purpose-built to shield sensitive information from adversaries positioned to exploit it.
articles.summaryHtml: PriFi, or private finance, is not about absolute secrecy, and it’s not about evading regulations. It’s about user-operated financial infrastructure, purpose-built to shield sensitive information from adversaries positioned to exploit it.

toc.title: Threats inside the deal: Counterparty hazards
Outsiders to the transaction: Predatory hazards
Insider and outsider hazards across the transaction lifecycle
Blockchain infrastructure: Shifting the terms of transactional hazards
From hazard classes to transaction-level threat modelling

articles.bodyHtml:
Properly designing such defences requires first understanding the types of hazards that could threaten transactions at various stages of their lifecycle. This article considers two classes of threats: those inside a transaction (the counterparties) and those outside it (potentially anyone else).

The previous two Logos blog posts explore a framework for understanding PriFi, starting from two related ideas. Firstly, a transaction should be understood as a supply chain rather than as a single act of settlement: any deal or exchange proceeds through discovery, diligence, negotiation, contracting, ordering, settlement, and enforcement, with each link introducing its own costs, dependencies, and potential failure points. The second is that the credibility of the commitments supporting those links hinges on what makes them hold when circumstances change, distinguishing commitments sustained by incentives from those enforced through structural constraints.

This post goes deeper into the two hazard classes that can exploit vulnerabilities at each stage in the transaction’s lifecycle. Threats from either class introduce risk, and mitigating those risks introduces costs. Risk and cost represent barriers to entry for many market participants, limiting their willingness to transact in a market. PriFi is a design philosophy aiming to minimise them both by eliminating all unnecessary information exposure and dependence on centrally hosted infrastructure, which is vulnerable to exterior pressures or breaches.

Threats inside the deal: Counterparty hazards

It should come as no surprise that those inside a deal or exchange – the parties actually transacting – would represent a class of hazards that can potentially introduce risks. Transaction-cost economics has traditionally devoted considerable attention to this problem. Oliver Williamson describes opportunism as “self-interest seeking with guile”: a party may misrepresent what they are offering, selectively disclose information, fail to honour an obligation, or otherwise exploit a position created through exchange (Williamson, 1985).

What distinguishes the counterparty from other potential threats is that some degree of access is inherent in their role. Transactions require participants to reveal information to one another and, in many cases, to place assets, authority, or decision-making power within the other's reach. A purchaser needs information about what they are buying. A lender requires information regarding a borrower's ability to repay. Parties negotiating a trade must disclose something about the terms on which they are willing to transact. Without such access, many exchanges could not take place at all.

The same access can nevertheless create opportunities for exploitation. A seller's superior knowledge of an asset can make misrepresentation possible. A buyer who receives goods before payment acquires temporary control over value that still belongs to the seller. A party negotiating a transaction may learn information about the other's constraints, urgency, or asset valuation and use that knowledge strategically. None of these hazards requires the counterparty to have entered the transaction with the intention to defect. They arise because participation creates informational and operational positions that did not exist before the parties began dealing with one another.

These positions can emerge at several points in the transaction lifecycle. During diligence, a counterparty may possess information that the other side cannot independently verify. During negotiation, each party learns something about the other's preferences and constraints. Contracting requires the parties to formalise terms and, depending on the arrangement, may assign particular permissions or authorities. Settlement can require one party to release value before every aspect of the exchange is complete, while enforcement may depend upon one participant continuing to comply with obligations after the principal transfer has occurred.

The risk posed by insiders is, therefore, closely connected to a basic feature of exchange: cooperation requires exposure. The parties need enough access to evaluate one another, agree on terms, and carry out the transaction, but every additional piece of information or capability granted to another actor can also enlarge the set of actions available to them.

Commercial institutions have developed an extensive range of mechanisms for managing this problem. Contracts, warranties, collateral, escrow, auditing, fiduciary duties, reputation, and courts all respond, in different ways, to risks created by placing another party in a privileged position during exchange (Williamson, 1983; Williamson, 1996). More recently, smart contracts have made it possible to constrain certain forms of discretion directly through executable conditions, so that some outcomes no longer depend solely upon a participant choosing to honour an obligation.

However, even where execution can be structurally constrained, the underlying requirement for access does not disappear. Counterparties still need enough information and capability to discover one another, assess the proposed exchange, negotiate its terms, and authorise the resulting transaction. PriFi, therefore, has to account for a hazard class that cannot simply be removed from the transaction's informational environment: the people with whom the user is deliberately choosing to deal.

Outsiders to the transaction: Predatory hazards

The second hazard class consists of actors who are not party to the transaction at all. They have not entered into the bargain, received rights under it, or accepted obligations towards the participants. Nevertheless, they may still be able to affect the transaction if they acquire information that creates opportunities for exploitation.

This class includes a wide range of potential actors. A competing bidder may benefit from learning the terms of an offer. A trader may profit from knowledge of an acquisition or large order before it has settled. A thief may become interested in an asset once its value and location are known. An extortionist may alter their demands after learning what a target can afford to pay. In onchain markets, a searcher may use information about a pending transaction to construct another transaction that captures value from the original user's intended trade.

What unites these examples is not the identity or motive of the actor, but their position relative to the exchange. Unlike a counterparty, they have no legitimate need for the information in order for the transaction to proceed. Their relevance is realised when information escapes the set of relationships in which disclosure is necessary.

This class of hazard has received comparatively less attention in traditional transaction-cost economics. Williamson distinguishes between the governance structures used to organise particular transactions and the wider “institutional environment” within which those structures operate (Williamson, 1991). Often, a degree of commercial confidentiality can be treated as part of that environment. Company negotiations take place privately, banks and lawyers develop duties of confidence, sealed bids conceal competing offers, and firms keep their ledgers and commercial records away from general view. These arrangements are imperfect, but continue to provide protection – at a cost. Universal publication is not, typically, the default condition of exchange.

That background determines which hazards must be addressed explicitly by the transaction itself. If commercially sensitive information is difficult for outside actors to obtain, many forms of predation remain largely outside the immediate governance problem. Once the cost of acquiring that information falls, however, actors who were previously irrelevant to the transaction can become significant.

Research into mergers and acquisitions provides a useful illustration. Studies of pre-announcement trading have found evidence consistent with private information about impending deals being incorporated into prices before public disclosure, allowing informed traders to benefit from information that originated within the transaction but was valuable outside it (Madura & Ngo, 2014; Madura, Ngo, & Susnjara, 2014). The transaction may still be completed, but some of the value expected by the participants can be transferred elsewhere through information leakage.

This suggests a useful predation model. An outside actor generally requires some combination of information, capacity, and impunity. Information allows the actor to identify a target or opportunity. Capacity determines whether they possess the means to exploit it. Impunity affects whether the expected consequences of doing so are sufficient to deter action.

The three conditions are related, but information has a distinctive role because it often determines whether the other two can be directed towards a particular transaction at all. A rival bidder cannot respond to an offer it does not know exists. A searcher cannot trade around an order it cannot observe. A thief may possess the general capacity to steal without having any reason to target a particular asset until its existence, value, or location becomes known.

Information alone is not enough to produce predation. An observer still needs the ability and incentive to act. However, absolute transparency of sensitive details can transform an otherwise irrelevant actor into one positioned to exploit the transaction.

Insider and outsider hazards across the transaction lifecycle

The distinction between insiders and outsiders is not confined to one stage in the transaction lifecycle. Both classes can appear at different points, although the information, capabilities, and opportunities available change from one stage to the next.

During discovery, the principal insider risk concerns the prospective counterparty itself. A participant may misrepresent who they are, what they control, or their ability to complete the proposed exchange. At the same time, the process of searching for a counterparty can reveal intentions to outsiders. Knowledge that a firm is seeking a particular asset, supplier, source of financing, or acquisition target may itself carry strategic value.

During diligence, the informational asymmetry between counterparties becomes particularly important. One party may possess facts that the other cannot independently verify, creating scope for misrepresentation or selective disclosure. However, diligence also requires the concentration and exchange of commercially sensitive information, which can become valuable to actors beyond the transaction if it is exposed.

The same pattern continues through negotiation and contracting. Participants necessarily reveal something about their valuations, constraints, priorities, and willingness to transact. That information can affect bargaining between the parties, while knowledge of the same negotiations may allow competitors, traders, or other outside actors to alter their own behaviour. Contracting can also assign permissions, authorities, or access needed to formalise the agreement, creating positions that did not exist before the parties entered the relationship.

At the time of ordering, the relevant capabilities change again. Actors responsible for sequencing transactions can occupy privileged positions by virtue of their role in determining the sequence in which competing instructions are processed. Meanwhile, observable transaction intentions can create opportunities for parties with no role in the original exchange to act before settlement occurs.

Settlement is the point at which blockchain systems provide their strongest guarantees. Protocol rules can sharply constrain which state transitions are accepted as valid. Yet settlement can still reveal economically significant information about asset movements, counterparties, and transaction history to observers outside the exchange. Furthermore, if an exploit occurs before settlement and an erroneous transaction is submitted, the chain will settle it with near-absolute finality, heightening the importance of securing all prior links. The case of the Bybit exploit of around $1.5 billion in 2025 provides a compelling example.

Finally, enforcement introduces further dependencies. Parties, intermediaries, or institutions may retain authority over obligations that continue after settlement, while actors outside the original transaction may influence those institutions or exploit information generated by the completed exchange.

Seen across the lifecycle, the two hazard classes are, therefore, not tied to particular actors or technologies. They describe positions that recur wherever a transaction creates access for participants or exposes information to those beyond it. The precise threat changes from link to link, but the analytical distinction remains useful: Who is involved because the transaction requires them to be, and who becomes relevant because the transaction reveals something they can use?

Blockchain infrastructure: Shifting the terms of transactional hazards 

Public blockchains alter the conditions under which the hazards operate because transparency is not merely a side effect of their design. It is central to how their rules and state transitions become independently verifiable. A transparent ledger allows participants to inspect the system's state and determine whether transactions conform to shared protocol rules. This is what gives blockchain settlement its unusually strong guarantees: valid state transitions are accepted according to the network's rules, while invalid ones are rejected.

For counterparties, this can narrow the scope for certain forms of discretion. Where conventional exchange may depend on a participant or intermediary retaining the ability to decide whether an obligation is honoured and how it is performed, smart contracts can make particular outcomes conditional on rules that neither party can unilaterally override. The counterparty may still possess information or other forms of access, but the set of actions available to them at settlement can be more tightly constrained.

The same architecture changes the position of outsiders in a different way. In transparent blockchain systems, public verifiability is achieved through broad observability of transaction data and state. Information concerning balances, transfers, counterparties, contract interactions, and, in some cases, pending intentions can therefore become available not only to the parties involved in the exchange, but to any observer able to inspect the relevant infrastructure.

This represents a substantial departure from the informational environment in which most conventional commerce developed. Historically, transaction information was fragmented across private ledgers, banks, brokers, advisers, counterparties, and other institutions. An outsider seeking to understand a transaction often needed privileged access to at least one of those sources. On a transparent blockchain, information that once required such access may instead become trivially available through the system's ordinary operation.

The effect is to shift the terms facing both hazard classes at once. Insiders may have less room to manipulate the rules governing settlement, but outsiders face a much lower cost of discovering that a transaction, position, or asset exists. The architecture, therefore, constrains some forms of insider discretion while simultaneously broadening the set of actors able to observe economically useful information.

From hazard classes to transaction-level threat modelling

Once insiders and outsiders are treated as distinct hazard classes, threat modelling becomes less about identifying generic "attackers" and more about understanding the positions different actors occupy relative to a transaction.

At each stage of the lifecycle, the first question is who must participate for the transaction to proceed. These actors may be counterparties, intermediaries, advisers, sequencers, infrastructure providers, or other agents whose role gives them access to information, authority, or control. While such participation is integral to the deal itself, it can also create opportunities for opportunism.

The second question concerns actors outside those relationships. What information does the transaction reveal beyond the parties who need it? Who can observe that information, directly or indirectly? What can be inferred by combining it with other data? Most importantly, what new opportunities arise once the information becomes available?

This produces a more useful account of exposure than simply classifying information as "public" or "private". A communication may reveal little about the substance of a negotiation while still disclosing that two parties are in contact. A visible balance may say nothing about a holder's immediate intentions while revealing that the account is economically significant. A pending transaction may not disclose the legal identity of its originator, yet still reveal enough about the intended action for another market participant to respond.

The significance of a disclosure, therefore, depends upon the position it creates for the observer. Information that is necessary for one actor to fulfil a legitimate role in the transaction may give an unrelated actor a completely different set of opportunities.

For PriFi, this means that analysing transaction privacy requires looking beyond whether individual data points are concealed. The more relevant question is how information and capabilities are distributed across the lifecycle, which actors acquire them, and whether that distribution creates avoidable positions of advantage or vulnerability.

Making exposure visible with Muster

Dr Corey Petty's work on Muster provides a practical environment for examining these questions. Muster is an experimental application built with the Logos stack for coordinating transactional activity within private conversations while making visible the information disclosed during the process and the infrastructure involved in carrying an action through to execution.

That makes it useful for moving from an abstract threat model to a more concrete examination of transactional exposure. Instead of considering a transaction only at the point where value settles, participants can inspect which information becomes available during coordination, which systems handle it, and where dependencies remain.

Viewed through the lens of the two hazard classes, those observations take on additional meaning. A disclosure can be examined not only in terms of what information becomes visible, but also in terms of who receives it and what position that actor occupies in the exchange. Some recipients are present because the transaction requires their participation. Others may become relevant only because information escapes beyond those relationships.

This distinction is especially important in systems where infrastructure itself can become part of the threat model. A frontend, communications service, routing provider, or other intermediary may not be an economic counterparty to the underlying transaction, but its role can still give it access to information or control that affects how the transaction unfolds. The previous Logos blog article introduced this broader question by identifying where coordination still depends on participants or infrastructure behaving as expected.

The purpose of mapping these positions is not to assume that every participant or observer is adversarial. It is to understand where the possibility of exploitation exists if incentives, circumstances, or actors change.

That is the value of separating the two hazard classes. Counterparties and outsiders can both threaten the gains from exchange, but they do so in different ways. One is admitted into the transaction because an exchange requires access. The other may become relevant because information travels further than the exchange requires.

Identifying those positions is the first step towards designing transaction infrastructure around a realistic threat model.

Explore Muster / Read Corey's post on transactional information exposure / Download Basecamp

This article is based on research compiled by Logos cofounder Jarrad Hope and ideas emerging from it. PriFi is central to Logos’ mission to revitalise civil society. Effective parallel organising requires economic rails that can withstand outside efforts to obstruct and manipulate activity.

toc.title: Time-based path selection for hidden services

articles.bodyHtml:
Logos provides monthly updates on the state of the technology stack and the development of its various modules, giving developers a clear snapshot of what has been built over the past month.

September closed with the release of Logos Testnet v0.3, bringing proof-of-work participation, decentralised sequencing, anonymous downloads, and the first wallets for existing assets to the stack.

The updates listed here are some of the most important highlights from the past month. Work progresses on many facets of the stack simultaneously, and a more complete, technical breakdown is available at roadmap.logos.co.

For developer-focused highlights on X, please follow Logos Tech. For broader updates on the Logos movement as a whole, stay tuned to the main Logos account.

Logos Testnet v0.3 is live

Logos Testnet v0.3 was released on 30 September, with improvements across almost every part of the stack, from how new participants join the network to how files and messages move privately between peers.

Node operators should update their clients, and developers will need to update existing LEZ programs, since the move to incremental state updates is a breaking change. The node operator guide covers running a node on the new release.

With the launch of testnet v0.3, EmPoWering is now operational, allowing new participants gain testnet tokens on the Logos Blockchain by performing computational work, which removes the centralised, traceable on-ramps networks usually rely on.

The Logos Execution Zone now supports decentralised sequencing, which sees a set of sequencers taking turns proposing blocks on a schedule enforced by the Logos Blockchain, each checking the blocks the others produce.

Logos Storage can now also route downloads over the Logos Mix network. At this initial stage, file providers are not yet shielded by the Mix network. Delivery now uses Rate-Limiting Nullifiers through the new RLN module, and RLN, Mix, and Service Discovery also now ship as standalone modules.

Other major updates in the latest version of testnet include Logos SQL, a distributed SQL database that runs as a Logos Blockchain zone, and Channel Notes that allows tokens bridged on the base layer to be staked by a zone’s sequencers.

Basecamp also now includes Monero and Ethereum testnet wallets, the latter with a verified proxy that checks each RPC response against cryptographic proofs.

The Logos Mix Network specification

The Logos Mix Network specification has been published, setting out the configuration of the anonymisation layer that Logos services run over. It is an opinionated instantiation of the libp2p mix protocol suite, so any node that follows it can operate as a Logos Mixnet node and interoperate with the rest.

All nodes are equal participants, meaning that for a given message a node may be the sender, an intermediary or the exit. Paths are three hops long with each node chosen at random from the discovered pool, every node must hold an RLN membership in order to send or forward, and each hop verifies the proof it receives before generating a fresh one for the packet it passes on.

Poseidon2 in circom-rln and Zerokit

A Poseidon2 circuit was shipped in circom-rln with an accompanying benchmark report, and Zerokit has added Poseidon2 examples for Rust, C, Nim and JavaScript along with FFI and WASM support.

Zerokit is the zero-knowledge toolkit behind RLN, the rate limiting that keeps spam off Logos Messaging without requiring identities. Hashing is the dominant cost in generating those proofs, so cheaper hashing means cheaper proofs on every client that produces one.

Time-based path selection for hidden services

A new discussion opened on the research forum covering time-based path selection for hidden services over the Logos Mixnet. 

Two designs were tested for how well they resist de-anonymisation: sampling complete paths with per-path rotation, and a fixed sparse topology with degrees configured according to the anonymity required.

The Mix path selection specification is being defined on the back of this work.

The de-MLS boundary contract

A new research discussion was opened on the de-MLS boundary contract. 

De-MLS runs a decentralised MLS conversation driven purely by the application that calls it, and the document examines what it guarantees at each of its boundaries, to the application, to the consensus service, and to MLS.

λPrize winners

Three builders won λPrizes this month.

pramadanif built a private multisig for the LEZ. Members approve spending from a shared fund, and the chain records that enough of them agreed without revealing who.

Timidan built DistributionX, a private airdrop. People claim from a list without the list, or their place on it, ever becoming public.

aegonmyy built an AI agent that runs on the Logos stack with its own private wallet. It spends within a limit its owner sets, and asks over encrypted chat before going beyond it.

Logos Broadcast Network and Circles

Throughout September, Logos contributors continued to host online and IRL Circles around the world, creating digital and physical space to solve real-world problems with privacy-preserving technology.

The Logos Broadcast Network continued to deliver regular programming, from Dev Club sessions and weekly technical updates to office hours every Friday at 14:00 UTC. Join these office hours to learn more about building on the Logos stack or to get help with specific issues.

Full schedules and participation details are available at press.logos.co/calendar and logos.co/circles. For a full list of upcoming Logos events, check out the event page on Luma.

To get the latest developer updates from the Logos stack, follow Logos Tech on X. Stay tuned to the main Logos account for news on the wider global movement.

Logos Circle / Mumbai cleans up Kharghar Hills

articles.bodyHtml:
Logos Testnet v0.3 release

In September, Logos Testnet v0.3 was released, with improvements reaching almost every part of the stack, from how new participants join the network to how files and messages move between peers.

With EmPoWering live, participants can now get testnet tokens by performing computational work rather than requesting them centrally from a faucet. Logos Storage now allows downloads over Mix, and Basecamp added Windows support while also getting early versions of Ethereum and Monero wallets.

Other additions in Testnet v0.3 include Logos SQL, a distributed SQL database run over a blockchain channel, and Channel Notes, which allows tokens bridged on the base layer to be staked by a zone’s sequencers.

Learn more about Testnet v0.3 / Run Basecamp and explore Testnet v0.3 / For more Sept dev updates

Local-first full-stack privacy

The Logos stack is engineered for truly private finance (PriFi). PriFi is a system design philosophy that aims to secure the entire transaction lifecycle – the steps involved in making any deal, transfer, or exchange that occur before and after settlement. Blockchain secures settlement uniquely well, but absolute transparency onchain introduces leaks at other links in the cycle.

Capital risks and the costs of protecting against them pose a barrier to entry for many market participants. PriFi infrastructure is engineered to disclose information only to necessary parties and shield by default. It runs P2P on users’ computers to minimise reliance on vulnerable proprietary hardware, while employing mechanisms to provide maximum privacy across the stack. By reducing costs and risks across the lifecycle, PriFi provides greater confidentiality and thus security than was previously attainable only by a wealthy few.

Learn more about PriFi / Explore why PriFi matters   

Local Area Network launches

September saw the relaunch of the ever-popular Logos zine. Local Area Network is a monthly snapshot of the movement as it flourishes. The first issue brings together tech updates, parallel organising news, Logos Circle win spotlights, a Monero thoughtpiece, and much more. 

Local Area Network celebrates those who are building or acting on Logos, spotlighting wins to inspire and fork for use across the network. It is built collectively as an archive of all our successes and learnings.

For Local Area Network to be the true voice of the movement, it needs the thoughts of many. Send field reports, technical walkthroughs, essays, data, visuals, lessons learned, and working prototypes to pressengine@logos.co.

Read Local Area Network: 01 The Founding Issue / Contribute to Local Area Network

Past becomes Present: Michael and Amanda’s stories

Past. Present. Future. is an initiative highlighting why infrastructure like Logos has never been more important and, if historic trends are anything to go by, is going to get a lot more important.

In Past, we went to the Museum of Civil Liberties, an Arctic archive of major events that resulted in the encroachment of personal freedoms. In Present, we follow three very different stories: Michael, Amanda, and a still-unrevealed character. As the player makes each character’s major decisions, three very clear symptoms of a society in rapid decline emerge. 

Michael’s story is about debt and how it restricts our choices. We join as he considers whether to borrow money to go to university or go straight into employment. Amanda’s story revolves around social media harms and how her health declines as her data is used against her. 

Play “Life’s Choices” / Visit the Museum of Civil Liberties

Building the parallel with Ethereum Philippines

Last month, Ethereum Philippines teamed up with Logos for a hands-on technical workshop, “Building the Parallel”, led by Alisher. The session introduced attendees to the Logos stack, the design process behind it, and practical ways to start building on Logos.

Those watching learned how to run a Logos node, install Basecamp, and support the tech’s development through opportunities like RFPs and λPrizes.

IRL / Upcoming

Freequencies

Logos is supporting the launch of Freequences in Lisbon on 7 October. The three-month programme of gatherings brings artists, performers, technologists, and collectives together to share skills, collaborate, and build stronger connections across the local scene. 

Freequencies is developing shared tools for coordination, archiving, communication, and event organisation on the Logos stack. The aim is to create infrastructure that Freequencies can use itself, while also enabling other cultural collectives to adopt, adapt, and self-host similar tools without relying on proprietary hardware controlled by Big Tech platforms.

Join us in Lisbon on 7 October

Field Station / Rajasthan

Field Station / Rajasthan opened applications in September and will bring together 30 residents for an eight-day builder-and-activist residency at Dhun, Rajasthan, from 23–31 October. Created as a collaborative effort by Logos and Zu-Grama, the programme invites developers, researchers, founders, and activists to cohabit while building and experimenting with social coordination on decentralised infrastructure.

Residents will work across two tracks: the Logos sovereignty and privacy stack, and Zu-Grama’s d/acc track, spanning AI, neurotech and bio-resilience. The residency is designed around practical outcomes, with participants running infrastructure, building prototypes, and tackling real civic challenges, including privacy-preserving mutual aid and local reporting.

The programme will culminate in a summit and showcase on 31 October, where residents will share what they built during the week. Applications are open to both technical and non-technical participants interested in contributing to a hands-on experiment in building more resilient, local-first communities.

Learn more about Field Station / Apply to Field Station

IRL / September

Dark Prague

From 2–4 October, Logos attended Dark Prague, bringing a three-day programme built around privacy, parallel infrastructure, and hands-on participation. Rather than treating it as a conventional conference, Logos created a working space where attendees could install Basecamp, spin up nodes, troubleshoot technical issues, explore PriFi, and contribute directly to the stack.

The programme combined technical workshops with Logos Circles, talks, and discussions on parallel organising, privacy infrastructure, and community-led alternatives to centralised systems. Attendees were encouraged not just to learn about the ideas behind Logos, but to leave having done something practical: running infrastructure, contributing to development, joining a Circle, or helping to start a new one. 

Jarrad Hope, Logos cofounder, also presented “Vaults of Glass”, in which he explored blockchain as an incomplete institutional breakthrough. Blockchain is uniquely strong on settlement but weak at protecting the six other links in a transaction’s lifecycle. The Logos stack is engineered specifically to secure it all.

Rounding the event off on Saturday evening was the Logos LAN Party with local dev collective Bordel. Running alongside the main Dark Prague rave, it combined hacking, music, conversation, and cryptoanarchist culture. 

Logos Circles

September highlights

Logos Circles are open, community-led groups that bring people together around local challenges. They develop practical, grassroots responses, connect their work with the wider movement, and draw on Logos technologies where they can meaningfully support their collective actions.

More about Circles / Find a Circle near you / Propose a new Circle

In September, Circles formed in:

/ Port Harcourt / Uyo / Awka / Kano / Lisbon / Zanzibar / Ruse / Vizag / Bauchi / Kampala / Madrid / Minna / Ibadan / Kaduna / Maiduguri / Wukari / Lokoja / Keffi / Mumbai / Sokoto / Katsina / Maraba / London / Jos / Aba /

Check the Logos Forum for individual progress updates on each Circle’s winnable issues

Logos Circle / Gombe expands access to preventative health care

On 20 September, Logos Circle / Gombe held a genotype awareness and free testing initiative at ECWA Urshalima Bagadaza in Gombe State. The Circle worked with four medical scientists and seven community volunteers to provide health education on genotype compatibility and sickle cell disease, while collecting 49 specimens from community members for genotype testing.

The outreach was designed to make preventive health information and basic testing more accessible, particularly for young people who may not know their genotype status. It also marked the first phase of a broader community health initiative, with Logos Circle / Gombe planning to expand similar practical, community-led interventions to other communities across the state.

More information

Logos Circle / Mumbai cleans up Kharghar Hills

On 27 September, Logos Circle Mumbai turned a problem identified at its first gathering into its first winnable issue: a trail cleanup in Kharghar Hills, Navi Mumbai. Seven members spent the morning clearing plastic bottles, glass, wrappers, cans, and other waste from the trail, ultimately removing more than 30 bags of rubbish from one of the city’s most heavily used green spaces.

The cleanup also drew in people beyond the Circle itself. Walkers on the trail helped carry filled bags back down, making the effort a small example of how visible local action can encourage wider participation. After the cleanup, the group met over lunch to discuss what Circle #3 could tackle next, with ideas ranging from another cleanup to initiatives around fitness and mental health.

More information

Logos Circles are already planned in the cities below in October:

λPrize winners

Three developers were awarded λPrizes in September. Pramadanif built a private multisig for the LEZ: members approve spending from a shared fund, and the chain records that enough of them approved, but no identifying information about them. 

Timidan built DistributionX, a private airdrop distributor tool where people claim from a list without its contents going public. And Aegonmyy built an AI agent that runs on the Logos stack with its own private wallet and that spends within a limit its owner sets, asking the owner over encrypted chat before exceeding it.

λPrizes support independent developers and contributors building useful, open-source projects on the Logos stack. Participants can submit work that strengthens Logos infrastructure through reusable technical contributions and demonstrable real-world progress, with eligible submissions considered for discretionary awards.

Learn more about the λPrize programme.

Logos Media

Blog

The Logos Blog shares technical updates, movement news, and longer-form perspectives on parallel organising and the ideas that shape it. If you have a topic or point of view you’d like to contribute, send us a proposal.

In September, we published: 

  • Field Station / Rajasthan: A Coliving Residency to Build the Parallel
  • PriFi and the Incomplete Institution: Securing the Transaction Supply Chain

Logos Broadcast Network

Each month, the Logos Broadcast Network brings together voices from across the movement to exchange ideas, expertise, and perspectives. Programming ranges from community gatherings to technical developer streams, conversations about emerging forms of coordination, and deeper explorations of the Logos stack and related technologies.

Check the Logos Broadcast Network calendar to see upcoming streams

Ideas

Every Thursday, Logos Broadcast Network invites voices from the movement and allied organisations to share their ideas and stories. These philosophical sessions aim to introduce concepts underpinning the parallel society movement and further the conversation around reclaiming agency and upholding freedoms with decentralised, local-first technologies.

Then, on the last Thursday of each month, the Sovereignty Superspace welcomes Parallel Society coalition partners and other big names from the intersection of tech and activism to discuss approaches to parallel organising. 

September streams included: 

  • Policy, Palantir, and Sound Money (with Susie Ward of Bitcoin Policy UK)
  • Mycelia Networks for Liberating Computation (with Jeff Emmett, author of MycoFi)
  • Parallel Lives: Card Counting, Occupy Activism, and Cypherpunk Nomadism (with Dave Stann)
  • Sovereignty Superspace (with Nym, DarkFi, and Cake Wallet)

Follow Logos on X or YouTube to join these discussions every Thursday

Technical

The Logos Broadcast Network also connects developers with the wider community through a regular programme of technical streams. In September, sessions included

  • Dev Club (Lambda Prizes, RFPs, vibe coding)
  • Tech Update (Testnet v0.3 Preview)
  • Dev Club (local-first agents, coding P2P poker on Basecamp)
  • Dev Club (bridgeless ETH to LEZ atomic swaps)

  • Dev Club (who sees your multisig payment?)
  • Tech Update (λBlockchain)
  • Dev Club (P2P poker on Basecamp, four open λPrizes, and more)

Follow Logos Tech on X and subscribe to the Logos YouTube channel to take part in all technical streams.

Builder Meetup

Logos Builder Meetups are bi-weekly sessions designed to help the community better understand, use, and build on Logos. Join every Friday at 12:00 UTC to speak directly with Logos engineers, ask questions, and develop a deeper understanding of the technology stack. The next one is on 9 October.

Circles

Logos Circle / Online is a weekly space for people taking on real challenges in their local communities. Each session combines practical guidance on starting a Logos Circle with insights from participants who are already organising and putting ideas into practice.

Logos Circle / Online is on Tuesdays; join us via the Logos X account or Logos YouTube channel.

Community champions

Logos is shaped by the people who choose to build, research, organise, and contribute. Whether through technical work, new ideas, community leadership, or hands-on participation, each contribution helps us progress, strengthen the network, and turn collective action into real-world wins.

These community champions went above and beyond in September: 

  • Mmlado for their work on spel-freeze-authority.
  • Terricola for continuing to build Field Wallet.
  • Pramadanif, Timidan, and Aegonmyy for their successful λPrize submissions.
  • Guru for their work across Logos and particularly on P2P poker for Basecamp.
  • Eden for developing Logos Forum, a serverless forum for Logos Basecamp.
  • Impure.zk for writing a beginner's guide to running a Testnet node.
  • Everyone helping Ibadan, Accra, Lagos, Gombe, and Mumbai Circles progress on their winnable issues.
  • Anyone already running Testnet v0.3.
  • All the stewards hosting Logos Circles in September, and everyone who attended.
  • Anyone building in stealth mode on Logos tech.
  • Everyone who joined a Logos Broadcast Network stream or read a Logos Blog article.

Your work could be featured in an upcoming community spotlight. Technical and non-technical contributions are equally welcome, so share what you’re building, researching, organising, or improving on the forum or Discord. 

Find a way to contribute, create something useful, and help move Logos forward. Build the parallel.

articles.summary: Testnet v0.3 introduces proof-of-work onboarding, decentralised sequencing for the LEZ, downloads over Mix, Logos SQL, and new Monero and Ethereum wallets in Basecamp.
articles.summaryHtml: Testnet v0.3 introduces proof-of-work onboarding, decentralised sequencing for the LEZ, downloads over Mix, Logos SQL, and new Monero and Ethereum wallets in Basecamp.

toc.title: Staking bridged funds with Channel Notes

articles.bodyHtml:
Logos Testnet v0.3 was released on 30 September 2026. The release brings improvements across almost every part of the stack, affecting everything from how new participants join the network to how files and messages move privately between peers.

To try out the new features in Logos Testnet v0.3, download and install the latest release of Basecamp.

Node operators should update their clients to the latest version with the launch of Testnet v0.3, and developers will need to update existing LEZ programs, as breaking changes have been introduced by significant improvements to the state update model.

This article outlines the key highlights of the changes introduced in Testnet v0.3, along with a brief look at what these new features do.

Information on running a node on Testnet v0.3 can be found in the node operator guide.

View the full list of updates in the release notes here. Below are the key highlights included in Testnet v0.3.

Proof-of-work participation with EmPoWering

To take part in a proof-of-stake network, you first need testnet tokens, which usually come from a faucet run by the project. 

EmPoWering adds another route in, letting new participants take part in Logos Blockchain by performing computational work and receiving testnet tokens from the network for such work.  

This removes centralised, traceable on-ramps to the network and means nobody needs to approve a request before a new participant can hold tokens and start transacting.

Read the full LIP for Proof-of-Work participation on Logos.

Decentralised sequencing for the LEZ

A sequencer decides the order in which transactions are included, and many layer-2s rely on a single sequencer that can see every transaction before it is final and halt the network if it goes offline. 

The Logos Execution Zone (LEZ) now supports decentralised sequencing, where a set of sequencers take turns proposing blocks on a schedule enforced by Logos Blockchain. 

Each sequencer checks the blocks produced by the others, applying valid ones and rejecting the rest. Indexers also rebuild the zone's state independently, so a sequencer cannot pass off a forged or replayed transaction.

For more on how decentralised sequencing is used in Logos Blockchain, read the documentation.

Downloads over Mix

Logos Storage can now route downloads over the Logos Mix network, with RLN providing spam protection, so the node downloading a file cannot be linked to the content it downloads. 

At this stage only the downloader is protected, as nodes providing files are not yet anonymised, and performance improvements are planned for upcoming testnet versions. 

Logos Storage also now works as a backend for the Logos package manager, allowing users to fetch packages from the Storage network instead of relying primarily on GitHub.

Read more about data transport over Mix.

RLN in Delivery

Delivery now uses Rate-Limiting Nullifiers (RLN) through the new RLN module, allowing each sender to prove they are within their message allowance without revealing which member they are. 

RLN proof validation will be switched on roughly two weeks after release, to allow a smooth transition. 

RLN, Mix, and Service Discovery also ship as standalone modules that can be more easily integrated with others, and Chat now uses RLN and Mix through Delivery.

Learn more about the RLN LEZ module.

Staking bridged funds with Channel Notes

When funds are bridged into a zone such as the LEZ, they are held on Logos Blockchain as notes belonging to that zone's channel. 

With the newly introduced Channel Notes mechanism, the zone's sequencers can stake those bridged funds on the base layer, so value bridged into a zone helps secure the base layer the zone relies on.

Logos SQL

Logos SQL is a new zone that turns a blockchain channel into a distributed SQL database. 

Developers write SQL transactions to the channel, and each node applies them to a copy of the database kept locally on its own machine. We welcome developers to start building database-backed applications with it now, using the SQL they already know. 

The testnet is still under active development and the network may be reset, but because the SQL database is stored locally, it can be rebroadcast after a reset, or when mainnet launches, instead of being rebuilt from scratch.

LEZ incremental state updates

The state update model for the LEZ has changed. LEZ programs now describe account changes as incremental diffs, recording only what has changed, instead of writing out the full state of every account after each update. 

This is faster and simpler for developers, and it is a breaking change, so existing LEZ programs will need to be updated. 

The change has been on the roadmap for some time, and feedback from building on the LEZ made it clear that large breaking changes are better made now, while the ecosystem is small, than later. 

Developers should expect some disruption at first, with smaller breaking changes possible in Testnet v0.4, after which breaking changes to the LEZ are expected only where security requires them.

Monero and Ethereum wallets

Basecamp now includes a Monero wallet, with balances, sending with a review step, receiving by QR code, transaction history, and wallet management. 

It also includes EVM wallet apps and modules, including an Ethereum wallet, a JSON-RPC client, a keystore, a signer, a token lists manager, and an Ethereum verified proxy. 

The verified proxy runs an Ethereum light client within Logos and checks each RPC response against cryptographic proofs, so a provider that returns false data produces an error instead of a wrong balance. 

Together, these let people who already hold Monero or Ethereum-based assets manage them from Basecamp on their own machine, providing a local-first alternative to centralised wallet services and RPC interfaces.

Other changes in this release

In Logos Core, logosctl has been added as a new single command-line tool that replaces logoscore, lgpm, and lgpd. Basecamp and Logos Core now also run on Windows, with an installer and a portable mode.

In Basecamp, applications can call one another through intents and deep links, the Blockchain Dashboard and explorer have been given a refreshed interface, and there have been general stability and interface improvements.

Chat now keeps message history across sessions, Delivery can retrieve messages missed while offline from store nodes, and the Reliable Channel API can split large messages and reassemble them on arrival. Note that accounts do not yet persist across different Chat sessions, and reopening chat creates a new account. Account persistence is coming soon.

Mix is also now available to developers through the Messaging API, and the Mix module allows node operators to run mix nodes.

In the LEZ, public transactions now carry transaction fees, zones can exchange messages asynchronously, and programs support events, upgrades after deployment, and deployment sharding. Bridging withdrawals are also included.

On Logos Blockchain, uncle references improve Cryptarchia's estimate of total stake, the Blend Network has a first version of message compression and failure detection, and the mempool specification has been published.

Read the full Testnet v0.3 release notes.

Getting started

Testnet v0.3 is available now. To run the stack and the new wallets on your own machine, download and install Basecamp at logos.co/basecamp.

If you want to run a node and contribute capacity to the network, or you are running into issues with setting up your node, see the node operator guide.

Developers can start building on Logos SQL and the LEZ today. Read more about the architecture of the Logos stack at docs.logos.co.

If you have questions, feedback, or ideas about what Logos is building, join the conversation on the Logos forum.

Build the parallel. Prove it in practice. Keep it human.
