toc.title: Muster on Logos: Showing privacy leaks across the transaction lifecycle
Logos Circle / Wukari supports local orphanage

articles.bodyHtml:
Museum of Civil Liberties opens

In August, Past.Present.Future., a new initiative exploring the systems that shape our freedoms and the forces that continue to erode them, went live. It begins with The Past and a trip to the Museum of Civil Liberties, an online museum tracing pivotal moments when our agency over money, communication, and political expression was weakened. The museum is a reminder of why privacy-preserving, censorship-resistant technologies are at the heart of Logos.

Enter the museum to explore the events that brought us here, from the end of the gold standard and the expansion of post-9/11 surveillance to internet shutdowns and the weaponisation of personal data. 

The Past is only the beginning: The Present and The Future are coming soon, extending the story of our eroding freedoms and where we’re heading if we don’t change course. 

Enter the Museum of Civil Liberties.

Raising chat control awareness 

Last month, Logos launched a new initiative examining the EU and UK’s latest efforts to regulate online safety through private-message scanning and age verification. Both are presented as targeted measures to protect children, but in practice they require much broader systems for inspecting communications or verifying the identities of ordinary users.

The initiative presents peer-reviewed research, large-scale empirical studies, and evidence from leading cryptographers and security researchers to show why these measures will fail at their stated goals while imposing significant threats to privacy and freedom. This is a core reason Logos exists: to build privacy-preserving, censorship-resistant technologies that uphold freedoms structurally rather than waiting for policy promises that rarely result in lasting change.

Check out the chat control initiative homepage.

If you’re local, join Logos Circle / London to support.

Muster on Logos: Showing privacy leaks across the transaction lifecycle

This month, Corey shared Muster, a sample application built on Logos to explore what privacy looks like across the full lifecycle of a transaction, not just at the point where value moves onchain. The demo brings encrypted messaging, coordination, negotiation, and private settlement into a single workflow, while also surfacing where information is exposed along the way.

Muster provides a useful demonstration of the PriFi thesis: protecting a transaction at settlement is not enough if intent, counterparties, terms, or identity leak through the tools used before and after it. By keeping more of that activity within the same privacy-oriented infrastructure, Logos can reduce dependence on fragmented, centrally operated services, and give users greater visibility and control over what they reveal. 

Learn more and experiment with Muster.

Parallel Dispatch launches

Parallel Dispatch is a new biweekly newsletter that highlights developments threatening our freedoms and the tech and people defending them. Expect a curated selection of topical stories covering legal updates, activist movements, and resistance technologies from around the world. Sign up at the bottom of the Logos homepage. 

Parallel Dispatch also features bite-sized interviews with pioneers building, theorising, or taking action to support the parallel society movement. The first was with Ann Brody, an interdisciplinary researcher and digital rights advocate whose work explores how decentralised technologies shape governance and collective organising.

IRL / Upcoming

Over the coming months, Logos is exploring plans for a linked series of residencies, technical gatherings, and cultural activations focused on privacy, coordination, and developing real world solutions on sovereign infrastructure.

Potential activities include hands-on experimentation with the Logos stack, community-led organising, and collaborations with artists and independent networks. Stay tuned for updates. More details will be shared as plans develop,

IRL / August

Zanzalu

Over three weeks at Zanzalu, the Logos community put both its technology and its approach to grassroots organising into practice. Participants explored Basecamp, learned how to get Logos nodes online, joined permaculture training, and connected with local projects to share skills and learn from existing community initiatives.

A highlight was returning to Straight Training Center, a community-run school supporting more than 120 students in Zanzibar. Last year, Logos Circle / Zanzibar helped raise funds for 10 Raspberry Pis to equip its computer room. This year, the team saw those computers in use, delivered children’s books collected through Logos Circle / Lisbon, ran English reading and conversation classes, and took part in music and cultural exchange sessions with students.

The visit also helped lay the groundwork for what comes next. Footage was captured for a short film to support future fundraising, while the Zanzibar Circle began looking at how it can help the school achieve its next major goal: constructing a permanent base to give the centre greater stability and room to expand. Learn more.

Logos Circles / August Highlights

Logos Circles are open, locally led groups where people come together to turn shared concerns into practical action. Members identify issues that matter in their communities, build grassroots responses, and connect those efforts to the wider global network, using Logos technologies where they add value.

  • More about Circles
  • Find a Circle near you
  • Propose a new Circle

In August, Circles formed in:

/ Awka / Lisbon / Kano / Zanzibar / Ede / Abeokuta / Khartoum / Abuja / Vizag / Calabar / Aba / Monrovia / Katsina / Kampala / Ibadan / Delta / Kaduna / Wukari / Yoal / Zaria / Sokoto / Gombe City / Bauchi / Maraba / Keffi / Benin / Minna / Ilorin / 

Check the Logos Forum for individual progress updates on each Circle’s winnable issues.

Logos Circle / Wukari supports local orphanage

On 29 August, Logos Circle / Wukari held its first community outreach at Success Orphanage Home in Pwadzu. Sixteen members took part, bringing food, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets, and donated clothing, while also meeting with the orphanage matron to better understand the home’s most urgent needs.

The Circle identified major challenges around clean water, overcrowding, and access to education, and arranged two volunteer maths and English tutors. The group is now planning a follow-up focused on beds and mattresses, water access, medical screenings, and additional hygiene support. Learn more.

Logos Circles / September

Logos Circles are already planned in the cities below in September:

  • / Portharcourt (3 Sept): Get involved.
  • / Uyo (5 Sept): Get involved. 
  • / Awka (5 Sept): Get involved.
  • / Kano (5 Sept): Get involved.

Several Logos Circles are still putting the finishing touches to their September plans, so only a handful of gatherings are confirmed at the moment. Check the Logos events calendar or the Circles discussion channel later this month for the latest events near you.

No Circle in your area yet? Get involved and start one.

Tech stack highlights

In August, two new releases of Logos Testnet v0.2 were shipped in quick succession, delivering iterative improvements. Logos Storage also pushed an update that brings better NAT traversal to node operators, making it considerably easier to run a node from a home network.

Two long-running pieces of work reached completion during the month. Zerokit v3.0.0 was released, completing the rearchitecture of the zero-knowledge library that powers RLN across Logos and the Status app, and the Logos Oracle Zone specification was finalised.

A faster network transport passed its scale testing, and message reliability went live in Status Communities, where messages that would previously have gone missing are now recovered automatically. Logos Core also saw an important security change, moving privilege out of the Basecamp interface so that no part of what a user sees on screen holds system-level access by default.

Research continued across network measurement, post-quantum readiness, and cross-zone coordination.

Logos Media

Blog

The Logos Blog features ongoing technical updates, movement news, and longer-form thinking on parallel organising and the ideas behind it. If you have a topic or perspective you’d like to contribute, send us a proposal.

In August, we published: 

  • Interzone Bridging: Moving Value Between Zones on Logos
  • Running Logos Basecamp is Easy, as the HodlUp Podcast Found Out
  • Parallel Education and Effective Community Action in Delhi

Logos Broadcast Network

Each month, the Logos Broadcast Network creates space for people across the movement to share ideas, knowledge, and perspectives. The schedule spans community sessions such as Logos Circle / Online, developer-focused technical streams, discussions on new models of coordination, and deep dives into the Logos stack and the technologies surrounding it.

Check the Logos Broadcast Network calendar to see upcoming streams.

Ideas / Parallel Lives

August saw the first instalment of a new format on the Logos Broadcast Network. Parallel Lives invites those living outside the system to discuss their stories. It replaces our previous Thursday philosophical sessions three weeks out of every month.

Then, on the last Thursday of each month, the Sovereignty Super Space welcomes Parallel Society coalition partners and other big names at the intersection of tech and activism to discuss approaches to parallel organising. 

August streams included: 

  • Surveillance as a Service (with Matt and Jason of Free Thought Project)
  • Parallel Lives: RPGs, Nomadism, and Privacy (with Kenny Palurintano)
  • Sovereignty Superspace (with Cake Wallet’s Seth, DarkFi’s Amir Taaki, and Nym’s Alexis Roussel)

Follow Logos on X or YouTube to join these discussions every Thursday.

Technical

The Logos Broadcast Network also connects developers with the wider community through a regular programme of technical streams. In August, sessions included:

  • Logos Dev Club (Lambda prize updates, Persona wallet, and chess on Logos Basecamp)
  • Logos Dev Club (P2P apps built on Logos)
  • Inside Logos Mixnet
  • Logos Dev Club (multisig on Logos, Muster exposes privacy leaks, encrypt everything with Keycard)
  • Proof of Work Onboarding and Decentralised Sequencing

Follow Logos Tech on X and subscribe to the Logos YouTube channel to take part in all future technical explorations and demos.

Office hours

Logos Office Hours are weekly sessions designed to help the community better understand, use, and build with the Logos stack. Join every Friday at 12:00 UTC to speak directly with Logos engineers, ask questions, and deepen your understanding of the technology stack.

Logos Circle / Online

Logos Circle / Online is a weekly space for people taking on real challenges in their local communities. Each session combines practical guidance on starting a Logos Circle with insights from participants who are already organising and putting ideas into practice.

Logos Circle / Online is on Tuesdays; join us via the Logos X account or Logos YouTube channel.

Community champions

Logos grows through the people who contribute to it. From developers and engineers to researchers, builders, and community leaders, every contribution helps advance the mission, strengthen the network, and turn shared ideas into meaningful action.

These community champions went above and beyond in August: 

  • ParadoxComputer for their continued work on Zonescan, a block explorer for Logos Execution Zones.
  • [NODERS] for their work on a block explorer and faucet for the Logos testnet.
  • Guru for shipping Xenia, a serverless AI inference marketplace over Logos Messaging. 
  • Bristin for their work stress testing Logos Zones.
  • Vladimir for connecting Alisher with Russian- and English-speaking communities to host Logos node-running workshops.
  • Austine for their inspiring medical care fundraising initiative. 
  • Amelia and Paschal for all their hard work in Zanzibar.
  • All the stewards hosting Logos Circles in June, and everyone who attended.
  • Anyone building on Logos tech.
  • Everyone who joined a Logos Broadcast Network stream or read a Logos Blog article.

Your work could be featured in an upcoming community spotlight. Technical and non-technical contributions are equally welcome, so share what you’re building, researching, organising, or improving on the forum or Discord. 

Find a way to contribute, create something useful, and help move Logos forward. Build the parallel.

 

Logos builds technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Come build the parallel with us.

  • Build on Logos. 
  • Write for Logos Blog.
  • Join a Logos Circle.

toc.title: Community action and parallel organising with Logos Circle / Delhi

articles.bodyHtml:
The most impactful community initiatives rarely start with endless planning behind closed doors. That’s what legacy institutions do, and if it were effective, we wouldn’t need Logos Circles. Instead, they start by getting out there, finding the people who need support and listening to the challenges they face. Logos Circles / Delhi did exactly that. Their work with a local volunteer-led education initiative is truly inspiring and should serve as a blueprint for others to follow.

Their approach perfectly encapsulates what Logos Circles are: self-organised local groups taking practical action on issues that matter to their communities. They don’t wait for permission to get stuck in. For Logos Circle / Delhi, that meant supporting a group of volunteers already teaching children at risk of falling through gaps in the Indian capital’s education system, in the open air – literally under a tree – and asking what would help make their work more stable.

The Circle began with a site visit: sitting in on classes, speaking with the volunteers and children, identifying challenges, and running a small drive for notebooks and learning materials. Going forward, Logos Circle / Delhi aims to help turn the informal tuition group into a stable community learning hub, with a reliable tutor roster, a fixed schedule, consistent supplies, basic learning-progress tracking, and eventually a space that can keep classes running through Delhi’s monsoon season.

They quickly moved from identifying the problem to getting involved in an easy but high-impact way. The Circle didn’t take on something grandiose and try to build a solution from scratch. They found an existing community initiative and asked how they could help it survive and grow. The Circle is also running a Logos node and beginning to explore where the Logos stack can strengthen the coordination layer around the project.

Logos Circle / Delhi’s steward Devisha shared what they’ve learned about effective grassroots planning and how their approach can be replicated elsewhere.

Community action and parallel organising with Logos Circle / Delhi


Hey Devisha, thanks for taking the time to talk about the work Logos Circle / Delhi is involved with. Let’s dive right in.

Hi. Yeah, let’s do it!

 

How did you discover the education initiative, and why did you pick it to focus the Delhi Circle’s energy on first?

We found it through a friend, who saw that these classes were going on near society in an open ground, where a group of volunteers were already running open-air tuition classes for children in Delhi NCR, quite literally under a tree. No building, no funding, no institution behind them. Just people who decided these children shouldn't go untaught.

We picked it because it was already alive. When our Circle sat down to choose a winnable issue, a lot of ideas on the table were things we'd have to build from zero; this one wasn't. The community had already responded to a failure of the formal system by organising its own answer. It just had no support structure to keep it standing.

That felt like exactly the kind of thing a Circle should exist for. We're not there to arrive with a solution and tell a community what it needs. We're there to find something people are already doing against the odds and make it durable. It's also unambiguously winnable: we can't fix education in Delhi, but we can help one learning group go from fragile to stable, and we'll be able to point at the difference.

Can you briefly describe the problems with education in and around Delhi?

The headline numbers make Delhi look better than it is. Enrolment is high, and the secondary dropout rate is around 4.8%, which sounds manageable. But two things hide underneath that.

First, being enrolled and being educated are not the same thing. India's larger learning crisis is well documented – large numbers of children sit in classrooms for years without reaching grade-level reading or arithmetic. Delhi has historically scored below the national average on learning outcomes, and it sits in the middle band on the government's own Performance Grading Index for 2025-26. The Delhi government itself has said it is working to identify around 750,000 students with learning gaps. That's an admission of scale from the system itself.

Second, the children we work with often don't appear in the statistics at all. Migrant families, children of daily-wage workers, kids who dropped out between Class 5 and Class 6, children whose families move between cities and lose their school seat in the process. 

There were roughly 30,000 students in one year alone who finished Class 5 and never entered Class 6. Those children don't show up as a dropout crisis in a dashboard. They just quietly disappear from the pipeline.

There's also a capacity problem. Vacant principal and teacher posts in Delhi government schools have been flagged repeatedly. So, even the children inside the system are often in overcrowded classrooms with no individual attention. The gap isn't only access. It's attention.

 

Does the education initiative that the Circle is supporting target a specific student demographic? 

Yes. For now, we're focused on students in grades 7 to 10, and that's a deliberate decision driven by what we can actually deliver well.

Our volunteers currently have subject expertise in maths, English, and science at that level. We could have spread ourselves across every age group that turns up, but we'd have done it badly. Teaching a Class 9 student science and teaching a six-year-old to read are completely different skills, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. We'd rather do a narrow thing properly than a broad thing thinly.

There's also a timing argument for this band. Grades 7 to 10 are where children are most at risk of falling away permanently; it's the stage where accumulated gaps become unmanageable, where the pressure to start earning kicks in, and where a child who's struggling decides school isn't for them. Catching someone at Class 8 who is two years behind is hard, but very doable. 

This is a starting point, not a policy. As we onboard more volunteers with different subject strengths, particularly foundational literacy for the younger children, we'll widen the age range. The constraint is our capacity, not the need. The need is for every age.

 

Is the education based on a specific curriculum, or is it more general to allow disadvantaged children to catch up?

It's a mix, and the balance shifts by student. Because we're working with grades 7 to 10, the NCERT/state board syllabus matters. These students are heading towards board exams, and teaching them something disconnected from what they'll be assessed on would be unfair to them. So, the subjects our volunteers teach – maths, English, science – track the standard curriculum for those grades.

Sitting in on the classes, this was one of the things we specifically went to understand: what they teach, in what order, and where it breaks down. The honest answer is that the curriculum is currently held in the heads of the volunteers rather than written down anywhere. That's one of the gaps we want to help close: not to impose a syllabus from outside, but to help them document what they're already doing so it survives any individual volunteer leaving, and so progress can actually be measured.

How was the Circle's help received by the organisers and children?

It was our first session, so we just went, sat, listened, and asked questions about what are the gaps in their education.

Five of our volunteers spent the day with around 65 children in genuinely brutal heat. We sat with them, went through what they were learning, and ran a small supplies drive: notebooks and basic materials.

The organisers have been doing this without help for a long time. Our position from the first conversation was that they are the institution and we're there to make their work sustainable. Once that landed, the conversation became very practical very quickly: what they actually need, what breaks every month, what they've never had time to fix.

The children showing up at all is the part I'd emphasise. Nobody makes them come. There's no register, no consequence for skipping. They walked through 40-plus degree heat because someone said there'd be a class. That tells you the demand isn't the problem.

 

Is Logos Circle / Delhi’s initiative reproducible by other Circles? How should Circle stewards go about doing so?

Very reproducible, probably more than most Circle projects, because the pattern doesn't depend on anything specific to Delhi. Almost every city has a version of this: a community already running something the state should be running, held together by a handful of unpaid people.

What I'd tell another steward:

  1. Look for what already exists before you invent anything. The instinct is to design a project. Walk your area and find the people already doing the work. Supporting an existing effort is faster, cheaper, and far more likely to survive than launching your own.
  2. First visit: Sit, watch, ask. You'll learn the real problems, which are almost never the ones you assumed.
  3. Talk to the organisers as partners. They've solved problems you haven't thought about yet. Ask what breaks: the answers are more useful.
  4. Choose a winnable version. Not “fix education”. Ours is: in six months, turn an informal tuition group into a stable learning hub with fixed schedule, tutor roster, progress tracking, reliable supplies. Small enough to actually finish.
  5. Fix consistency before you fix anything else. A predictable weekly slot is worth more than a large one-off donation. Most of these efforts don't die from lack of money; they die from irregularity.
  6. Document from day one. Baseline numbers, photos, notes. 

 

What would make the biggest difference to the children’s education if it arrived tomorrow?

Three things, in this order:

Committed volunteer tutors. This is the binding constraint. Five volunteers for 30-45 children is not a ratio at which anyone learns to read. Ten reliable people who show up every week would transform outcomes more than any amount of equipment. And “committed” matters more than “qualified”. Consistency beats credentials with these children.

A monsoon-proof space. Right now, the classroom is a tree. That works for part of the year, and then it doesn't. A shared room, a community hall, even a covered courtyard would take an entire category of disruption off the table.

A recurring supplies pipeline instead of one-off drives. We did a notebook distribution and it was lovely, but it's not a system. A small, predictable monthly budget sponsored by a few people rather than donated in a burst would mean nobody has to teach without materials again.

 

Is there scope for Logos technologies to be incorporated into the initiative?

Yes, but not with the children, as most of them don't have phones or computers; the beneficiaries are not online, but the technology serves the coordination layer around them. That layer is real, and it has real problems:

  • Tutor and volunteer coordination. 
  • A materials archive on Logos Storage. 
  • Transparent community funding. For the supplies pipeline and eventually the learning space. We're watching what Circle / Benin built with FundBrave, and Circle / Abeokuta is using. Small-donor education funding in India has a real trust problem: people want to give but don't believe that the money actually arrives. Transparent, auditable allocation is a direct answer to that.

 

How did you find the Logos node setup process? 

Honestly, it was more approachable than I expected. Running it through Basecamp meant I didn't have to touch a command line. It's a normal desktop install, and the node dashboard is built in. Also, thanks to Alisher for guiding me step by step on it. 

The Indian government plans to upgrade many school libraries and classrooms this year. What do you think? Will it close the gap? Will initiatives like Logos Circle / Delhi’s still be needed?

I think it's genuinely good news, and I don't want to be cynical about it. Delhi is upgrading 125 school libraries with digital devices and kiosks, and setting up thousands of smart classrooms. But it won't close the gap, for a simple structural reason: these upgrades reach children who are inside the system. The children we teach are outside it.

A smart classroom does nothing for a child who isn't enrolled. A digital library doesn't help a girl who left after Class 5 when her family migrated, or a boy whose parents need him working by afternoon. Infrastructure improves the experience of the enrolled. It doesn't reach the ones who fell out.

The children we work with don't primarily lack devices. They lack an adult with time who knows exactly where they're stuck. That's not something you can procure.

So yes, initiatives like this will still be needed, and I'd argue the two aren't in competition. The ideal outcome isn't that we replace the state; it's that we catch the children the state's programmes structurally can't reach, and where possible get them back into the system, ready to actually use those new libraries.

That's really what a parallel institution means to us. Not opposition, but coverage of the space the existing system doesn't reach.

 

Truly inspiring! Thanks for sharing your story, Devisha. Keep on doing amazing things.

Thank you! And anytime.

Inspired? Take action now

Logos Circle / Delhi is a testament to the power of grassroots collective action. They saw a problem and got to work. That’s the whole point of Logos Circles.

You can do the same in your local community. Propose a new Circle, take the steward training, and start making a difference where you live.

 

Join a Circle. Run Logos Basecamp. 
Build the parallel.

toc.title: Explore the Logos stack's base of operations
What can you do for Logos Basecamp?
Transcript: Why Privacy Can’t Be Bolted On In Crypto

articles.bodyHtml:
Long-time Logos evangelist Dr Corey Petty recently joined the HodlUp podcast to discuss privacy, parallel societies, AI, building better institutions, and where Logos is headed.

While the whole podcast is well worth listening to, the main take-home message was just how simple it is to run the Logos stack on hardware you control via Logos Basecamp. Find out below.

Basecamp is a fully local launcher for the complete Logos stack, running all default modules – Storage, Messaging, and Blockchain – along with installable modules and apps that expand its capabilities on a device you control. Learn more about Logos Basecamp.

Watch Corey on the HodlUp Podcast.

Logos development progress 

Logos Testnet v0.2.1 is live, and most of the core stack is functional, including execution environments and private atomic swaps.

Development is beyond "wait for testnet launch" and into the "harden and grow" phase. And for that, the network needs real usage, not just sideline spectators. Run Logos Testnet v0.2.1 now. 

Explore the Logos stack's base of operations

Running Basecamp to get started with Logos is easy:

  • Just download Basecamp and click run. That's the entire install.
  • Basecamp requires minimal system specs: a Raspberry Pi is enough.
  • It’s going to get even easier to run: more deployment options are on the way, so you won't need to dedicate your main machine to it.

What can you do for Logos Basecamp?

You can help harden the Logos stack. Get involved by:

  1. Trying to break it. Run a node, play around with it, file any issues you encounter.
  2. Building on it. The stack is ready for you to use. Get involved.
  3. Applying for a grant. RFPs are open for contributions that expand Logos’ usability and functionality.

Why building on Basecamp matters

The more developers building on Basecamp and exploring its capabilities, the sooner we'll arrive at the mainnet release. Simply running a node through Basecamp increases the anonymity set for all users, and building novel modules for Basecamp can reveal bugs in the code that need to be addressed before the network goes fully live. 

As Corey mentioned on the HodlUp Podcast, the bar for Logos’s success isn't a roadmap item shipping on time; it's someone building something the engineers behind it never anticipated. Logos is meant to be built collectively in the open, not developed behind closed doors. 

  • Watch Corey on HodlUp
  • Download Basecamp
  • Explore developer grants and open RFPs

Basecamp video tutorials

If you’re not ready to dive in and explore Basecamp yourself yet, the video tutorials below show just how easy it is to get it up and running and start your journey.

  • Quickstart Logos Basecamp
  • Installing Logos Basecamp
  • Understanding .lgx Modules on Logos Basecamp
  • Building Your First “Hello-World” UI Module on Logos Basecamp

If you’re struggling with anything Basecamp-related, you can put your questions to the engineers who built it during Logos Office Hours. They’re every Friday at 12:00 UTC. Attend an office hour.

You can also ask for help at any time in the Logos Discord.

What's already running on Basecamp

Since the Logos Testnet v0.1’s release in March, developers have been busy building new modules and sample applications for it. The examples below may not have been updated to run on the latest version of Basecamp, but they do show what’s possible with the stack and will hopefully inspire the development of new modules.

  • IA Archiver: Preserve Internet Archive items on Logos Storage. Learn more.
  • Anon Forum: An old-school anonymous forum on local infra. Learn more.
  • Receiver: A sovereign internet radio module. Learn more.
  • DOOM on Basecamp: Run the legendary shoot-em-up inside Basecamp. Learn more. 

We're building technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Come build the parallel with us.

  • Run Logos Basecamp.
  • Read the docs.
  • Join a Logos Circle.

Transcript: Why Privacy Can’t Be Bolted On In Crypto

Atis Shala: Hello Corey, how's it going?

Corey Petty: Going well. Happy to be here, good to meet y'all. I was looking you guys up, doing some background research, and I think this is going to be a fun conversation.

Atis Shala: Definitely. Considering you joined crypto in 2013, if I'm not mistaken, this is going to be a long one. Before we get into everything else, I want to ask you the question I ask everyone: what got you into crypto? What was the idea behind you joining? It's a whole world out there, and crypto has changed so much over the years.

Corey Petty: I might take up our whole time with this one. I originally did a PhD in computational physics, and I've always been fascinated with computation. My PhD was in high-performance computing, so solving really hard computational problems was something I cared about. I've also always been a deconstructionist: I like taking things apart and putting them back together with as few pieces as possible.

By happenstance, I saw a TED talk about Bitcoin while I was doing my graduate studies, and I was fascinated by it. I liked the computational problem it was solving, the Byzantine Generals' Problem, and I thought the solution was elegant. So I researched it, wanted to understand the ins and outs, wanted to see how it could break down. Then I started playing with it, and I learned about money and the weirdness that is money. I found it fascinating that we'd built real, sovereign internet money, something we'd never had before. It was a fundamentally new thing to me, and I got lost in it.

I started mining because the best way to learn is by doing, and the more competent I became, the more fascinated I got. Eventually, I started a podcast and met a lot of people through great conversations – that's The Bitcoin Podcast… shameless plug. I really enjoyed it, and eventually I left academia, because the problems I was solving there, while interesting, were problems nobody cared about. Meanwhile, this huge industry was emerging that I saw as an exponential technology about to take off, one that gives power back to people. I care a lot about cryptography, information, and decentralised systems, so I got a job doing data science and blockchain education, then moved into security.

Then I got a job at Status after their ICO, where I was lead security engineer and CSO. I kept doing it because the ecosystem kept exploding, and I was always trying to build things I believe in: resilient systems built for adversarial settings, resistant to being taken over. That's core to who I am: figuring out how to build systems that aren't asymmetric in power.

Dren Hima: I resonate with that. When we joined crypto, we were drawn in by the same philosophy. You've lived through the most important cycles this space has seen and watched it evolve into what it is today. Do you like it? Did you predict this is where it would end up? It doesn't feel the same anymore. I get nostalgic about a lot of things, but especially about when we first joined crypto. We can talk all day about ideology and institutions, but it just doesn't feel the same. I want your take, because I know you've been critical of the institutionalisation of crypto.

Corey Petty: No, I don't like it, but I'm not surprised by it either. The ideology isn't gone. When we started The Bitcoin Podcast, our whole line was "adoption is the only thing that matters." We were going to replace the banks, give people ownership of their own financial data. But that's not the adoption we got, because it's genuinely hard to do. Using a wallet, taking responsibility for your own private keys, understanding what you're signing, understanding what chain your tokens are on, navigating the weird dynamics of DeFi – all of that is hard, and people don't like hard. It means learning something new and changing their behaviour.

So the adoption we got was driven by scale and convenience, and a lot of what we built ended up being the same thing we already had, just on the internet: traditional finance, online. That isn't what I signed up for, but it's clearly the direction things went, because it's what people wanted. We haven't yet convinced them of the thing I got into this for, and why they need it. I think we're getting there. People are starting to realise this isn't fundamentally different from what came before. I'm still hopeful we can build something that actually feels better than what we already have.

Atis Shala: On the institutionalisation of crypto, I think it was inevitable, like you said. But I also think we asked for it, in a way. Maybe not you specifically, but the majority of the industry. Back in 2020 and 2021, whenever there was news of some new institution getting into crypto, everyone got fired up. I think the industry has an identity crisis around this, and it connects to privacy too, because I think anonymity and privacy in crypto should be non-negotiable.

Corey Petty: I'd agree.

Atis Shala: But how realistic is that? Regular people don't really care, do they? If you ask my parents whether they care that their data gets sold from their social media accounts to feed algorithms that essentially enslave them digitally, they wouldn't care. I try to say I care, and I try to stand behind the movement, but it's hard to stay idealistic in today's world. How would you convince someone to fight this fight? I see it almost as a war: How do you get people to stand behind these values?

Corey Petty: That's a hard one. Honestly, I don't think you convince most people directly. This mirrors something I saw doing security work: people only care about security once it's already been breached, once it personally affects them, and by then it's usually too late. So, as builders, we have to be the ideological ones and build things that don't give people the option to skip these protections. It has to be built into the substrate, the infrastructure itself, so people are protected by default and have to actively opt out if they want to. That's consent, versus the current model, where consent was never really given.

Privacy is the same story. The transparency baked into everything we use today creates a surveillance economy, and the easiest way to profit from that is to aggregate data and exploit it; the user becomes the product. Companies aren't building for what users need; they're building to take advantage of them, because that's what the current substrate incentivises. So I'm less interested in trying to "sell" privacy and anonymity, and more interested in building a substrate that doesn't give people that choice to be exploited by default, one where they have to actively consent, and in some cases can even profit from their own data instead of someone else scraping it because that's the cheapest option.

You can't bolt privacy onto a system after the fact – or you can, but it's much harder. The lifecycle of a transaction has many steps, and if you think of the blockchain as the settlement layer, that's the end of the lifecycle. Almost all the surveillance and profiteering happens before you ever get there. So it doesn't matter if you have a privacy solution on the blockchain if everything's already been harvested upstream, or if bad actors just go after whoever's using the privacy solution instead. You have to secure and privatise the entire transaction lifecycle, so the user can choose when to disclose information, instead of having it sold off before they ever had a choice.

Dren Hima: That's exactly it. People did ask for mass adoption. They did ask for institutional money to come in. It's like asking for rain and getting a thunderstorm instead.

Corey Petty: A monsoon.

Dren Hima: A monsoon with a lot of narratives and political battles thrown in, though we don't need to go down that rabbit hole right now. I want to ask about Logos and the philosophy behind it. You mentioned pivoting away from academia. I imagine you had to unlearn a fair amount from that world to get to where you are now, building Logos and everything that comes with it.

Corey Petty: I don't know that I've unlearned so much as stopped using it the way I originally learned it. I've actually come full circle on this: I think institutions really matter. But you need to build good ones, because institutions are what survive across generations; they carry forward core ideas and complex thought, and train new people to keep doing that. So you need to rebuild institutions in a way that makes them uncapturable, which requires the right infrastructure underneath them.

What we mostly see today are captured institutions. The goal is to rebuild them so they're resistant to capture. That's what we've been trying to do with blockchains: build technology that resists this asymmetric dynamic where a small number of people end up controlling the whole system. We've learned a lot over the past decade and a half about how to actually do that well, and maybe now we're at a point where we can build something that genuinely helps rebuild institutions in society.

Atis Shala: So, how do you actually plan to do that? Institutions keep getting built in ways that are easy to capture. I don't want to be the pessimist here, but it feels like almost anything can be bought with today's mindset – a lot of people are losing their ideals. Everyone you talk to about building something better ends up asking, "What's in it for me, financially?" I get it, it's a business, but we're trying to build something with a different kind of value, not just financial. How do you want to change that?

Corey Petty: A lot of our philosophy is: don't try to fix the existing system, build something in parallel that gives people options, purpose-built for what they actually need, instead of trying to bend something that was never designed to serve them. And you have to build those things so they can't easily be captured or broken.

That means resilient technology that gives people the tools to build their own communities and parallel institutions in their own niche areas, and then supports that growth. Ideally, what emerges are resilient institutions that actually serve real people, instead of the detached systems we have now.

It starts with building technology that's provably resistant in real-world conditions, then going out, learning people's actual problems, and helping them build things that serve those needs, then fostering that community growth. I don't think you get real societal change unless you do both simultaneously: build uncapturable technology that serves people, and understand people's problems well enough to help them use it. Big problems only get solved by big communities, so you have to battle-test this stuff, let it grow iteratively, and keep the focus on actually helping people.

Dren Hima: As an economist myself, I put some blame on economists for this. We tend to assign statistical value to almost everything except privacy. You see projects shipping surveillance tracking in the backend that users have no idea about. But if you asked people how much they'd pay to have their data protected and be anonymous online, I'd bet most would pay something. So privacy can be monetised too.

Which brings me to AI. It's scaled a lot of good things, but also a lot of the bad, including surveillance. I'll be honest, Claude and ChatGPT know a lot about me because I'm the type of person who asks for help with the most minor things. I vouch for total privacy, and yet I'm clearly caught up in this too. I want to hear your take on AI. You've written about how it boosts efficiency, but are there hidden dynamics people aren't aware of, beyond surveillance and privacy?

Corey Petty: That's a big one. I'm fascinated by AI for a lot of reasons: how it works, the emergent property of it actually being able to reason, the environmental and social implications of hyperscalers, how people use and leverage it, and whether it makes them stop thinking or actually think better and become more efficient.

What worries me is the amount of control these hyperscalers actually have, and the potential, from that control, to manipulate society in ways that aren't obvious. You ask it questions the way you'd use a search engine, and it gives you an answer, but you don't know where that answer really comes from. It comes from how the model was trained, post-trained, served, and the rules the provider builds in. This is the first time in history a single company controls the entire information pipeline – from data aggregation to training to serving – and it's all proprietary. You don't really know how any of it works.

Historically, we've had multiple institutions and gatekeepers controlling different parts of an information pipeline, which gave us some checks and balances. That's gone now. These companies are also transnational and massive, so they're not really subject to any single jurisdiction. It's a scary, unproven situation. AI has real potential to make society better, but only if it's built with checks and balances we haven't figured out yet, and I don't think hyperscalers are the ones who'll figure it out. We also haven't solved how to make these systems capable enough without just scaling them bigger and bigger, with all the resources that requires.

So there's real potential for harm and real potential for good, and I'm caught in the middle. Computationally, it's fascinating. I love it, it makes me better at what I do, it helps me learn. But it can also make people dumber if they don't use it the right way. We'll see.

Atis Shala: I saw a post somewhere – "don't outsource your thinking to AI" – and honestly, I think I've been doing exactly that.

Corey Petty: Because a lot of the value in life is in the thinking itself. Struggling with an idea, wrestling with complexity – that's the point of the exercise. When you offload that entirely, you lose the capacity to do it.

Atis Shala: I think at some point you stop being human, in a sense. After a decade of outsourcing everything to AI, people just forget how to think, and that's the one thing that makes us human. I don't want to go too far down that road either. So, you said you're fascinated by AI, but how do we stay decentralised and keep these giants from taking over? Is local compute the answer to AI sovereignty, or are we too far from that?

Corey Petty: I think we'll find ways to decentralise training, inference, and data ownership and aggregation – the whole pipeline that feeds these models. Model sizes will shrink to the point where meaningful reasoning can run on devices people can actually afford, so it stops being a global scarcity problem over who controls the compute. It becomes something you can run on your laptop or phone, once we get better at doing this efficiently.

At that point, you're no longer dependent on hyperscalers, because there's an alternative. I've made this comparison with crypto before: I don't mind using Coinbase, because it's built on a decentralised platform. If I don't like what they're doing with my Bitcoin, I can move it onto the blockchain directly. I have the option to exit. If you don't have that option, a company can do whatever it wants, because you can't do anything about it. So whether we're talking about crypto or AI, you need a place to exit – a way to still do what you want to do, without being subject to any one company's rules. When people have that option, companies have to earn their users because those users can simply leave.

Atis Shala: I agree with all of that, but from your perspective, what role does blockchain play in a future where people run local, private AI? There have been a few blockchain projects aiming at more efficient data preservation than Bitcoin's chain, while keeping its core benefits. I remember one called MINA, back in 2021, though I'm not sure it still exists. I know the concept is out there, but is it actually being practised? Can blockchain support that future while staying private?

Corey Petty: Absolutely, that's exactly what Logos is trying to do. Blockchain plays a critical role in building decentralised, resilient applications by providing meaningful digital scarcity: I can give you something, and you know I no longer have it, because of global total ordering that everyone can agree on.

In an age where AI can manufacture almost anything, trustless verifiability becomes essential. I know something is mine, and it's provable – backed by cryptography, not by someone's word. Systems that operate reliably in adversarial conditions give me confidence something actually happened and that I can prove it. Add zero-knowledge proofs, and I can prove something happened correctly without revealing the underlying details. That combination – total ordering, verifiability, permissions, decentralisation that resists takeover, and privacy – is powerful. It matters when you work with people you don't fully trust, or when you're building communities that can't be captured because they don't leak the information needed to capture them.

Blockchains serve that role, but you don't put real data on-chain. The chain is just there to prove something happened, for as long as you need that proof. After that, you can checkpoint and archive it elsewhere, because the cryptographic linkage already guarantees immutability. That's what something like Logos Storage is for: keeping large amounts of data available long-term while staying private.

Where blockchains have historically lacked privacy is in the consensus and mining process itself, which leaks information and has led to people being coerced or robbed. So we believe privacy needs to be built in at the lowest level of the stack – where nodes actually run. I don't want to know your IP address, your stake, or your influence over the mining process; I just want to know the process is fair and verifiable. That's what we're doing with zero-knowledge proofs and what we call the Blend network – it hides who proposed a given block and also obscures the network forensics around how that block propagates. Even if you can't see what's inside the chain, existing "private" chains are still vulnerable because you can watch who's actually processing transactions and go after them. If you want this to hold up in the real world, privacy has to exist at the lowest level. We believe we've done that with Logos, but it still needs to be battle-tested and scaled.

Dren Hima: How do we keep bad actors away? A lot of the case for surveillance states rests on the idea that privacy enables crime, because authorities can't track bad actors – that's where a lot of the pushback on privacy comes from. Is it realistic to build a world with real privacy that's still safe from bad actors, without undermining the principles that made privacy possible in the first place?

Corey Petty: No, there will always be bad actors. There are bad actors today. The real question is whether the good this technology enables outweighs the harm those bad actors cause. I've always believed ethical people should be the ones building this technology, because if they aren't, the good guys end up playing catch-up to the bad actors' methods instead. Wherever a community reaches a certain size, you'll find people trying to exploit it; that's just how it goes. You build systems that minimise their impact and structure networks so no one can assert outsized control, because bad actors aren't going away. You want ethical builders creating the tools, and you help the people trying to stop bad actors by understanding how bad actors could exploit the system.

A lot of what bad actors need is information. If you don't hand it to them, it becomes much harder to do what they want to do, especially anything involving surveillance or exploitation of others. So no, you don't eliminate bad actors, but you build systems resilient to them, and help the communities using the technology root out bad behaviour where it exists. At the end of the day, it's humans on both sides of this technology, and humans make mistakes; you catch bad actors not by manipulating the system, but by watching the humans.

Dren Hima: I want to talk about the concept of parallel societies. What's the most concrete evidence, in your view, that parallel societies are real and not just a metaphor?

Corey Petty: That's really more Jarrad's territory; it's his whole thing. But I can offer a few examples. We already have special economic zones, which function as financially incentivised parallel societies outside normal jurisdictions. Unconventional communities are operating in international waters, doing their own thing – a modern echo of how piracy historically forced questions about jurisdiction and jurisdiction-free spaces. And throughout history, we've seen parallel institutions stand up to regimes and win – not through violence.

It's hard for me to push my own views here because I've always focused on the technology side of this. I like the idea of people having a right to exit, and spending their time in systems that actually benefit them instead of exploiting them. Jarrad's book, Farewell to Westphalia, has great examples of parallel institutions throughout history that worked: economically viable, sometimes producing real markets worth pursuing. This isn't just an idealistic social movement; there's real business opportunity in serving people this way. But I don't spend my time studying that side these days. I'm more focused on what emerges once we give people the technology to build it themselves.

Atis Shala: Let's look at the future of Logos. You have three products: Messaging, Storage, and Blockchain. What's still missing from the stack right now? I think the unification of the brand happened in late 2025. What's the next step, and what should people following Logos be excited about?

Corey Petty: We have testnets running, and most of the four core pieces are working: execution environments with DEXs, private atomic swaps, all the main components. Now we need to harden them, test them, and grow the user base building on top of them. The best thing anyone can do is download Basecamp, run a node, and either file a bug report or try to break it – or build something on top of it.

We have grant programmes and RFPs for people who want to help build, so it's not just us building this and handing it to people – it's meant to be a community effort. The best measure of success, honestly, is someone building something we never planned for. You can start today: download Basecamp, check the website, and look at the funded opportunities for things we want built but don't have the time or resources for ourselves.

Running a node is genuinely simple: download Basecamp, click run, and it can run on something as small as a Raspberry Pi. We have things in the pipeline to make that even easier, so you're not limited to running it on your main machine – you can deploy it to a small device at home, or rely on someone else's node safely, because our light-client protocols let you verify the data you're being given is correct.

Atis Shala: So, through the Lambda programme, I could go build something like Logos Markets – a prediction market – and get funded?

Corey Petty: If your proposal is solid, yes, we'll fund you.

Atis Shala: I might need your help putting that proposal together.

Corey Petty: Submit a proposal; the requirements are laid out clearly. I actually helped build the evaluation framework, so when people build something, they know exactly what they're building against, and it's easy to check whether it meets the bar. We want people doing this; we've allocated funding for it, because you can't do this alone. You need people building on it, with a real stake in growing the network alongside you.

Dren Hima: Zooming out – ten years from now, ignoring PR metrics and TVL numbers that have flooded my feed – what would tell you Logos succeeded? And what would tell you it didn't?

Corey Petty: Success, to me, looks like large communities actually using the Logos stack to run something they need – a land registry, a local market, a voting system, something meaningful and community-scale. That's real impact. I don't want to see another DeFi protocol that just shuffles money around and profits someone without doing anything else. I want real societal impact, and people getting curious enough to build new kinds of communities on top of it – genuine parallel societies, meaning communities of like-minded people who've opted in around shared values. As those grow, they need some form of bureaucracy to hold together, and the technology can serve that through registries, fair markets, voting mechanisms, and so on.

That's success. Failure looks like exactly where we are today – regulated stablecoins that don't actually serve people.

Atis Shala: I want to ask about Blend, since it's relatively new to Logos, and you mentioned how easy node setup is supposed to be. What's your plan for growing adoption of Blend nodes? It's a brutal market to grow in right now.

Corey Petty: Great question. This is something I've always cared about, because privacy exists in proportion to the size of the anonymity set, and there's a real bootstrapping problem: How do you build and maintain that set?

Here's the short version of how Blend works today: when someone wins the right to propose the next block in Cryptarchia, our consensus mechanism, they have to broadcast it to the network – and that broadcast leaks information. Over time, someone doing network forensics could de-anonymise who holds what stake just by observing how often they propose blocks, since proposal frequency is weighted by stake. That could expose someone's IP address and, ultimately, their physical location, which we obviously want to avoid.

Blend solves this by routing proposals through a network inspired by mix nets – though it isn't quite a mix net – introducing random delays across multiple hops, where each hop doesn't know who came before it. That hides who's submitting what. But you also need cover traffic, so not every message looks like a block proposal, or you can trivially tell which messages actually matter. Plain cover traffic, though, is just wasted bandwidth.

There's something new on the roadmap I'm comfortable discussing now, called EmPoWering – a neat way to solve several of these problems at once. The economics aren't fully worked out yet, but I'm writing that up now. The rough idea: a new node could do proof-of-work to hit a certain threshold and generate a small pool of funds that covers their first transaction on the Blend network, meaning you can gain entry and keep the anonymity set alive purely by contributing computation, without needing outside funding. This incentivises fresh accounts to submit real transactions instead of relying on synthetic cover traffic, and you can auto-tune the size of the anonymity set the same way Bitcoin auto-tunes mining difficulty, matching it against real network traffic.

That gives us real cover traffic made of genuine transactions, funded by proof-of-work rather than some external funding source that would otherwise dox you – say, by requiring a deposit from an exchange. It solves the bootstrapping problem: How do you enter proof-of-stake consensus without funding your node from a traceable source? You should be able to enter and exit the network freely, the same way you can with Bitcoin mining, without needing to fund anything up front. It's a genuinely new approach. Version three of Blend should include an early implementation in testnet, though the documentation isn't public yet. I'm writing a technical piece that covers the economics in more depth.

Atis Shala: So it's essentially a modular way to enter the Blend network.

Corey Petty: Right – it automatically tunes the security and efficiency of the anonymity set, and gives people an onboarding path that doesn't require funding a node before they can send a single transaction. You can mine your way into your first transaction.

Atis Shala: Looking forward to that write-up.

Dren Hima: How do we get the average degen trader into Logos? Privacy as a narrative is arguably having its best year yet: ZEC has had a moment, Monero keeps coming up, and there are more privacy-by-default chains launching. But how do we make it stick and bring in the next wave of users? We've had Session on the podcast before – a decentralised alternative to Telegram – and they're relying on donations because it's hard to scale something with real utility without eventually needing the average degen trader in the network.

Corey Petty: We need trading activity; things need to move for any of this to be sustainable, and people need to use it.

Dren Hima: Exactly, so how do we bring them in?

Corey Petty: I don't have a full solution, but I have ideas. One is building something efficient enough to support applications that genuinely can't be built elsewhere: a fully private transaction lifecycle that doesn't require negotiating a multisig transaction over Telegram, real private atomic swaps, and so on. Another is a developer experience that's second to none and unified across the whole ecosystem – interacting with Storage feels similar to interacting with Messaging, which feels similar to interacting with the blockchain layer. Because these pieces are merged, we can offer a seamless experience for building an entire application – chat, long-term storage, consensus, token swaps – all within one wallet, one integrated system.

If the infrastructure is solid and the developer experience is genuinely simple – without the usual glue code of stitching together Ethereum for one thing and Solana for swaps and something else for storage – that complexity mostly disappears. Good infrastructure, real guarantees, real control over when to disclose information, and ease of building on top of it: that's how you get people to build the applications that eventually pull in that next wave of users.

Atis Shala: Suppose you succeed in driving privacy adoption and build out a whole ecosystem around it, similar to what already exists for non-private blockchains, and then a government decides to ban anything connected to privacy platforms, threatening serious jail time for users, and other countries follow suit. Realistically, what can we do? I know Monero was recently delisted from most major exchanges. Is enough being done to engage policymakers and convince them that some of these regulatory approaches to privacy are wrong?

Corey Petty: I don't know how to solve politics. It matters a great deal because those decisions affect so many people. Even if the technology works perfectly, if using it becomes practically unusable because of the legal consequences, you won't get adoption: people will be too scared to use it. That's not a problem you fix by building better technology; it's a problem you fix by talking to people – your local representatives, your community. Ideally, when one jurisdiction gets something wrong, others call it out. Public pressure and reputational cost are really the only tools that have consistently worked to change behaviour, but that requires global coordination and people actually caring.

Part of our job, as builders, is proving this technology is genuinely good for people, so they demand it and go tell their own local representatives why they care. Without that grassroots demand, you don't get real political change – and to get that grassroots demand, we have to show people solutions that meaningfully improve their lives, not just talk about ideals.

Dren Hima: We've had a lot of guests on this show who are polished and media-trained, saying what they know how to say. It's rare to get someone who genuinely knows what they're talking about. Dr Corey Petty, thank you so much for joining us. This has been a genuinely eye-opening conversation, and I wish we had more time, because there's so much more we could dig into.

Corey Petty: Thank you, I appreciate that. There's so much to talk about; it's a fascinating space.

Dren Hima: It really is the most interesting industry in the world – chaotic; sometimes I question why I joined, but here we are, building asshole-resistant technology. Cheers to that.

Corey Petty: Thank you for having me; this was great!

Dren Hima: Thank you.

articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Extending imperative credibility beyond transaction settlement to reduce risks and costs

PriFi aims to secure the entire transaction supply chain.

articles.title: Logos Dev Update: July 2026
articles.subtitle: Your monthly update on the development of the Logos technology stack.
articles.summary: Following June's Testnet v0.2 release, July was a month of consolidation, with anonymous messaging over the mix network becoming usable and documented for the first time.
articles.summaryHtml: Following June's Testnet v0.2 release, July was a month of consolidation, with anonymous messaging over the mix network becoming usable and documented for the first time.

toc.title: Anonymous messaging over the mix network

articles.bodyHtml:
Logos provides monthly updates on the state of the technology stack and the development of its various modules, giving developers a clear snapshot of what has been built over the past month.

For developer-focused highlights on X, please follow Logos Tech. For broader updates on the Logos movement as a whole, stay tuned to the main Logos account.

Anonymous messaging over the mix network

The month's most significant milestone was making sender-anonymous messaging a capability developers can pick up and use. LIONESS payload encryption for Sphinx was merged into the mix protocol implementation and confirmed to integrate with Logos Delivery without issues, preserving message integrity end to end.

Documentation was then published covering how to send anonymised messages over the mix network on testnet v0.2, with messages routed sender-unlinkably through a three-hop mixnet via Logos Chat. Mix-based chat with DoS protection was also presented and demoed at the IFT Town Hall.

Logos technology stack updates

Logos Core

Basecamp moved to a dockable workspace layout, added keyboard shortcut handling and an ARM Linux build, and now presents a single install and upgrade confirmation dialog listing any dependency changes.

Storage

Storage research focused on hidden services, with a purpose-built simulator developed to model a hidden service over the mix network using guards and vanguards, followed by a free-route simulator for studying path selection and the malicious-path problem.

Work also progressed on NAT traversal ahead of Testnet v0.2.1, with several improvements made that significantly improve node connectivity.

Elsewhere, all wire protocols were migrated to nim-protobuf-serialisation in place of hand-written serialisers, and the Logos Storage UI was brought largely into line with the Logos Design System.

Messaging

The Messaging API progressed closer towards main feature completeness. RLN was isolated into a self-contained module usable by any protocol, the FFI node lifecycle was unified and the legacy surface dropped, structured API layers were introduced, and an in-repo end-to-end test suite was added.

Logos Chat advanced towards Beta with GroupV2 client integration, group names and descriptions, membership changes surfaced as events, and key bundles now published over Logos Delivery. The Reliable Channel API continued to stabilise, and the Rate Limit Manager moved into the messaging client layer.

Blockchain

Testnet v0.2 completed its rollout across the stack, with the Logos Blockchain node 0.2.0 released alongside the blockchain module and dashboard, the LEZ module, wallet UI, indexer, and explorer. An iterative update, Testnet v0.2.1, is expected to roll out on 5 August 2026.

On the Logos Execution Zone, a Keccak speedup for the Risc0 backend cut proving time by roughly half, and async cross-zone messaging reached review complete with a browser demo showing send, finalise, and receive timings live. Nimbos merged libp2p AutoNAT v2 and wired SDP validator operations into the ledger.

AnonComms

Two long-running research threads reached publication. The oracle mechanism specification is now published as a LIP, laying the groundwork for the Decentralised Oracle Network, and the payment streams on-chain specification was published alongside an end-to-end demo of payment streams with Store integration.

The Zerokit v3.0.0 rearchitecture is close to release, and a working RLN membership management module and UI were deployed on testnet, including an experiment using a Keycard device certificate as an authentication method.

Post-quantum benchmarks and research

Post-quantum work continued to be a recurring theme, with benchmarks of cryptographic primitives conducted on a Raspberry Pi 5 and Apple M3, and Blend post-quantum primitive candidates finalised.

An anonymous communications simulation framework with two closed-form anonymity predictions was built, a survey of turn-assignment mechanisms for channel sequencing was completed, and the Checkpoint-based Fast Bootstrapping RFC was opened for review.

Documentation

Logos Storage documentation is being revamped, with a view to eventually add it to the documentations available on docs.logos.co. A set of runnable tutorials was also added to the libp2p module, with continuous integration checks on the tutorial code.

A closer look at the user-facing launcher for the Logos stack was also published in Basecamp in Testnet v0.2.

The documentation for the Logos stack is maintained at docs.logos.co, and the Node Operator Guide remains the best starting point for running a node on Logos Testnet v0.2.

Logos Broadcast Network and Circles

Throughout July, Logos contributors continued to host online and IRL Circles around the world, creating digital and physical space to solve real-world problems with privacy-preserving technology.

Logos contributors also headed to DWeb in Berlin last month, where we hosted four days of talks, technical sessions, and fostering collective action to support human freedom. Check out this recap of the event on X.

The Logos Broadcast Network continued to deliver regular programming, from Dev Club sessions and weekly technical updates to office hours every Friday at 14:00 UTC. Join these office hours to learn more about building on the Logos stack or to get help with specific issues.

To help new users get started with downloading and using Basecamp, Logos has published a set of tutorials on YouTube.

Full schedules and participation details are available at press.logos.co/calendar and logos.co/circles. For a full list of upcoming Logos events, check out the event page on Luma.

To get the latest developer updates from the Logos stack, follow Logos Tech on X. Stay tuned to the main Logos account for news on the wider global movement.

articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Extending imperative credibility beyond transaction settlement to reduce risks and costs
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: Blockchains solved one of the oldest economic problems: how to make a promise hold even when the party making it would prefer otherwise. If security is concentrated at the moment value moves, while information and discretion remain exposed everywhere around it, the transaction remains vulnerable. PriFi aims to secure the entire transaction supply chain.

articles.title: Interzone Bridging: Moving Value Between Zones on Logos
articles.subtitle: How Logos Zones move tokens and messages between each other without a trusted intermediary.
articles.summary: Interzone bridging makes Logos Zones interoperable and links them to the shared, decentralised base layer.
articles.summaryHtml: Interzone bridging makes Logos Zones interoperable and links them to the shared, decentralised base layer.
articles.bodyHtml:
Bridges have been the most expensive thing in this industry to get wrong. Ronin lost roughly $620 million in March 2022 when five of its nine validator keys were compromised. Wormhole had lost $325 million seven weeks earlier to a signature verification flaw. Harmony's Horizon bridge lost close to $100 million on a two-of-five multisig that summer, Nomad around $190 million a month after that, and Multichain about $126 million in 2023 after its team lost access to the keys holding the pools. Cumulative losses across cross-chain bridges run into the billions.

The causes differ in the detail, but the underlying challenge is the same. Something has to stand between two chains and attest that a deposit happened on the far side, and that something — a relayer, a multisig committee, an MPC keyset — becomes the most valuable target in the system. Compromise the attestor and you are able to mint whatever you like.

Whether it is a cross-chain bridge or a cross-Zone transfer, this mechanism extends the supply chain of a transaction and consequently its privacy exposure surface. Conventional cross-chain bridges mitigate this exposure by inserting a party that both chains agree to believe, but protection is only ever as strong as its weakest link. In nearly every bridge that has been drained, that trusted party was exploited.

So now that Logos Zones can move tokens and messages between one another, the obvious question is: how does that work without a trusted intermediary?

What shipped

PR #542 landed on 11 July: asynchronous cross-Zone messaging between Logos Execution Zone (LEZ) instances, with two demos running on one shared messaging spine. The first is a minimal ping between Zones. The second locks tokens on Zone A and mints a wrapped representation on Zone B. There is also a two-Zone chat app that sends messages across and displays send, finalise and receive timings live in the browser.

This work is called “interzone bridging", but the mechanics have little in common with what bridging between different blockchains normally means. Here, it refers not to moving tokens between different networks, but different Zones that are designed to be interoperable and linked to the Logos base layer.

The shared base layer

Zones are customisable execution environments that lean on the Logos blockchain for consensus and data availability. The documentation covers what a Zone is and how Mantle channels anchor Zone state to the chain. A key property of this architecture is that every Zone reads the same finalised blocks.

Traditional bridges connect chains that share nothing. Ethereum has no idea what Solana’s state is, so somebody has to carry the news across, and that somebody has to be trusted. Every bridge design is some flavor of “who carries the news and why do we believe them.” Multisigs, oracle networks, light clients, they’re all answers to that question, and the first two have been the most expensive answers in the history of this industry.

Logos Zones never face that question. Zone B does not need to be told what happened on Zone A, because Zone A's activity is already sitting in a finalised block that Zone B reads as a matter of course.

How a message moves

The token bridge demo below shows the flow most clearly.

  1. A program on Zone A locks the tokens and records an outbound message through a built-in outbox program. That message lands in a finalised block like any other Zone A activity.
  2. Zone B's sequencer runs a watcher over Zone A's finalised blocks. When the outbound message appears, the sequencer injects the delivery into Zone B as a sequencer-origin transaction, and the wrapped-token program mints.
  3. Zone B's indexer then re-derives that same delivery from the same finalised block, independently. Both Zones run identical LEZ code, so the indexer can reconstruct what the delivery must be, byte for byte, and throw out anything that does not match. Forged deliveries fail. Replayed deliveries fail. The verifier pins Zone A's block-signing keys, so a fabricated source chain fails too.

This means the sequencer injecting the delivery is never trusted. It carries the delivery but holds no authority over it, because every injection is checked against what the finalised block says it must have been. A sequencer that injects invalid data gets its own block rejected by its own indexer.

There is no relayer committee here, no multisig, no oracle, no extra validator set, no new token to stake. Verification is re-derivation from finalised state, so the trust model of interzone bridging is simply the trust model of the chain underneath it. Nothing crosses between the two Zones, because both of them are already reading the same blocks.

Sequencing and atomic coordination

Two related threads of work make this picture more complete.

Sequencer decentralisation is the first. Today’s design gives sequencers a job (watch, inject) but no authority (the indexer verifies everything). The team is reworking zone sequencing toward stake-gated registration with round-robin turns and posting timeouts, so no single sequencer can stall a zone, and by extension stall its cross-zone deliveries. A malicious sequencer can’t forge deliveries now; a decentralised set means one can’t withhold them either.

Second, async messaging is one half of cross-zone interaction. The other half is the Cross-Zone Atomic Coordination Protocol, a four-phase off-chain protocol (intent proposal, verification, signature exchange, submission) for the synchronous case where two zones need to commit a transaction atomically. Both sequencers hold a complete signed transaction after the signature exchange, which removes the single point of failure of classical two-phase commit. That work is still at the specification stage, with a security analysis covering abort scenarios at each phase.

Either way, the principle is the same one the rest of the Logos stack is built on. Every link in the chain gets verified on its own terms rather than inherited on trust from the link before it, which is why one compromised component draining everything is not a failure mode this architecture has.

Scope and limitations

This is LEZ-to-LEZ only. Both Zones running identical code is the premise that makes byte-for-byte re-derivation possible at all. Bridging to arbitrary external chains is a different problem and this work makes no claim on it.

Cross-Zone messaging is opt-in and off by default. A Zone with no cross-Zone configuration behaves exactly as it did before.

This is also the first part of a larger design. Follow-up work will include generalised message envelopes, an emitter-agnostic watcher, refund handling, and a broader trust and discovery model beyond the two demo flows.

This mechanism is purely Zone-to-Zone: moving tokens between the Logos blockchain and a single Zone is a separate system, already live, built on Mantle channel deposits and withdrawals and covered in the documentation.

Get involved

To try interzone bridging:

Run the two-Zone demo from the PR, send messages between Zones, and watch the timings in the chat app;

Read the indexer-side verifier and the integration tests covering forgery, replay and ingress guarding, then open an issue if there is a hole in the design;

Or work through the documentation for more on Zones, channels, and how Zone state is anchored to the chain.

Build the parallel. Prove it in practice. Keep it human.

articlesFromSameAuthors.title: How To Ethically Build Public Goods Infrastructure
articlesFromSameAuthors.subtitle: Adhering to our principles is not an easy route, but it is necessary for ethically building public goods
articlesFromSameAuthors.summary: We are building infrastructure that optimises non-zero-sum interactions, aiming to disempower bad actors without compromising on our principles. For example, censorship may be an effective solution, but it results in capture and other consequences we oppose. In this article, I’ll outline how messages sent on the blockchain can be interpreted and censored, identifying the need for censorship resistance to be built into the very bottom of the technology stack. I’ll also discuss our transformation of the original Whisper protocol into the public good Waku, and how we infuse ethics into the open source protocols we develop.
